Completely positive maps describe how quantum systems change while probabilities stay sensible. James Tian gives a self-contained derivation of two structure theorems for such maps in 2025, the Stinespring and Kraus representations. The derivation uses only scalar positive-definite kernels.

Textbook proofs of these theorems often rely on heavier machinery from operator algebras. A kernel-only route makes the results reachable for readers with a more modest background. The theorems underpin quantum information theory, where Kraus operators are the standard way to model noise in quantum devices. Kraus operators are the form in which noise models are usually handed to engineers. Stinespring's theorem explains why those operators must exist in the first place.
arxiv-2512-00356:
Quantized transport is famous in gapped topological materials, but it can also appear in metals. Fan Yang and Xingyu Li study quantized nonlinear transport in Fermi gases with Berry curvature in 2025, and where that quantization breaks down. An earlier proposal linked a nonlinear conductance to the Euler characteristic of the Fermi sea.

The authors consider two-dimensional noninteracting fermionic systems whose Fermi surface carries nonvanishing Berry curvature. Berry curvature acts like a magnetic field in momentum space and bends how carriers move. Knowing when the effect survives helps lab teams read such tests in new quantum materials. Such effects grow with the driving field, which sets them apart from plain conduction. For folks who probe such stuff in the lab, the gain is a clear line. They can tell a true odd effect from a plain one, and trust the test.
arxiv-2512-00556:
Language models can echo social biases in subtle ways that simple guardrails miss. Sina Salimian, Gias Uddin, Sumon Biswas, and Henry Leung present a framework for bias testing and mitigation in black box language models in 2025. It uses metamorphic relations, rules about how outputs should change when inputs change.

Indirect or contextually complex prompts often slip past existing safeguards. A unified framework for systematic evaluation and targeted mitigation addresses both detection and repair. Because the models are black boxes, the methods work from observable behavior alone, which suits the commercial systems most people actually use. Metamorphic testing needs no ground truth labels, only relations that outputs must obey.
arxiv-2512-00656:
Claims that language models flatter and agree with users, called sycophancy, have multiplied quickly. Jan Batzner, Volker Stocker, Stefan Schmid, and Gjergji Kasneci review those claims in 2025 and find a missing human in the loop. They identify five core ways sycophancy has been operationalized.

Sycophancy is inherently human-centric: it describes how a response lands on a person. Yet current research does not evaluate human perception of the behavior it labels. Without that check, the field may be measuring artifacts of its own prompts, and the paper urges grounding the debate in what users actually experience. The missing human in the loop is the paper's central complaint and its title.
arxiv-2512-00956:
Jiale Chen, Vage Egiazarian, Torsten Hoefler, and Dan Alistarh present WUSH in a 2025 paper on model compression. Quantization stores language model weights in very few bits, shrinking the model for cheaper use. A few extreme weights and activations stretch the range and waste the quantizer's limited steps.

A common fix applies a fixed rotation, such as a Hadamard transform, before quantizing, which tames the extremes. WUSH instead learns adaptive transforms tuned to the model. Near-optimal transforms could keep quality high at very low bit widths. That would let large models run on smaller, cheaper hardware.
arxiv-2512-01856:
Eric Joyce and co-authors ask if image-based pose estimation can support robot grasping alone. Their frame evaluates estimators of six-degree object pose. Inputs are single RGB images, with no depth sensor. Accuracy is one question. Grasp readiness is the sharper one.

Tests show how pose errors pass into grasp outcomes. An estimator good on benchmarks may still fail a gripper. Linking pose scores to grasp success sets a real bar. Single-camera grasping would cut robot cost if that bar can be met reliably. Grasp trials run in simulation and on hardware, so benchmark poses are graded by physical success, not by numeric error alone.
arxiv-2512-02056:
Training a large language model is slow and expensive, so most users fine-tune an existing foundation model instead. Eshed Gal and five co-authors introduce in 2025 reversible architectures for these models, designed to use far less memory during training and fine-tuning.

The designs borrow from symmetric and symplectic differential equations, structures that can be run backward exactly. Reversibility means intermediate activations need not all be stored, since they can be recomputed in reverse, which is where the memory savings come from. The authors also study the theoretical properties of these architectures, testing whether efficiency costs capability.
arxiv-2512-02356:
An Earth twin transiting a distant star dims it slightly and briefly, a signal easily lost in the star's own restless noise. Shuyue Zheng, Fabo Feng, and Yicheng Rui developed SPLS in 2025, an algorithm that fits the transit and the background trend at the same time.

Segmented polynomial fitting by least squares models the background in pieces with a double polynomial, so the shallow, long-period dip of an Earth-like planet is not fitted away. Detecting such twins is among astronomy's hardest data problems, since the signal hides inside stellar variability. A cleaner separation of planet from noise brings the census of Earth-like worlds closer.
arxiv-2512-02456:
A vision-language model must both see accurately and reason soundly, and weakness in either caps the whole. Sourabh Sharma, Sonam Gupta, and Sadbhawna present in 2025 a self-taught multimodal reasoner, built to improve its own perception and reasoning together rather than importing the skill from outside.

Earlier efforts strengthened reasoning while leaving perception to chance, so models reasoned elegantly about things they had mis-seen. A self-taught loop promises gains without proportionally more labeled data. Multimodal systems that check their own seeing before thinking could become markedly more reliable on visual questions.
arxiv-2512-02756:
Milla Åhlfeldt and a large team squeeze a common protein and watch how it responds at the nanoscale. Pressure can reshape a protein's folded state, and high enough pressure unfolds it. Hydrated lysozyme, a small enzyme often used as a model protein, serves as the test case here.

Using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, the team measures stress relaxation as pressure rises toward four tenths of a gigapascal. The motion of the protein reveals how its soft structure yields. Results inform food processing and preservation, where high pressure treats products without heat. Food plants use hard squeeze in place of heat, so a clear view of what squeeze does to food pays off fast.
arxiv-2512-02856:
Min Soe and co-authors simulate a light pulse striking the boundary between two clear materials, using a quantum style algorithm. A bounded two dimensional electromagnetic pulse travels onto a plane dielectric interface. How it reflects and refracts tests the simulation method itself.

The qubit lattice algorithm runs as a sequence of unitary collision and streaming steps. With suitable potential steps, it recovers Maxwell's equations in uneven dielectric media to second order accuracy. Such schemes may one day let quantum hardware simulate classical waves efficiently and accurately. Wave tests with sharp edges are a stern check. A code that passes them here can be put to work on waves in air, sea, and glass with trust.
arxiv-2512-03156:
An old star near the end of its life has a restless atmosphere. K. Ohnaka and co-authors image the star W Hya in sharp detail in this 2025 work. They use ALMA, a large array of radio dishes in Chile.

The team observed with the array's longest baselines, giving very fine views. They probe how gas moves and what chemistry occurs in the star's air and inner wind. Dying stars seed space with the raw material for new stars and planets. Close views show how that material leaves the star. W Hya is close and bright, which makes it an ideal target for such fine imaging.
arxiv-2512-03556:
Robots that learn in one place often fail in another. Yinzhou Tang and co-authors present RoboScape-R in this 2025 work. Imitation policies overfit to expert paths, while reinforcement learning lacks a unified reward across scenes.

Their model unifies reward and observation world models for training. A shared reward signal supports generalization across diverse scenarios. Robots trained this way may adapt to new rooms and tasks more readily. General skills are key if robots are to leave labs for homes and warehouses. World models let robots rehearse in imagination, cutting risky real-world trial and error.
arxiv-2512-03656:
Salim Khazem and Houssam Kanso forecast electricity demand several steps ahead by teaching networks the calendar's rhythms. Grid operators live or die by these predictions. Their 2025 framework encodes dates and times as sine and cosine waves so weekly and yearly cycles stay visible to the model.

A hybrid ensemble pairs a memory-based LSTM with a pattern-spotting CNN, topped by small specialist regressors, one per forecast horizon. A year of national consumption data trained and tested the system. Ablation studies isolated what the cyclical encodings and calendar features each contribute. Across all seven horizons, the hybrid beat its own components and published baselines on standard error measures.
arxiv-2512-03756:
Self-driving cars must predict where nearby road users will go, then plan a safe path through that forecast. Marlon Steiner and colleagues study how to feed a car's own intended route into that prediction step. Their 2025 robotics preprint extends an attention-based prediction model with navigation information, including the destination pose the car aims for.

The team proposes several ways to wire route information into the model architecture and tests each on the nuPlan dataset of driving scenarios. Adding the route helps in two directions at once: forecasts of other agents improve, and the planned motion becomes more stable and physically feasible. Their results make the case for prediction-driven planning, where knowing the goal sharpens every other part of the driving stack. Code for the work is released publicly through the group's repository.
arxiv-2512-04056:
Quantum Monte Carlo simulations of electrons hit a notorious wall: the sign problem, where negative weights wreck the statistics. Ryan Larson, Rubem Mondaini, and Richard T. Scalettar study that bias head-on in a 2025 preprint. Their test case is the doped Hubbard model, where ignoring the sign flips a key result, making pairing look suppressed instead of enhanced.

Rather than hunting negative paths, the authors sort measurements by sign. They build histograms of kinetic energy, magnetic structure, and pairing responses for positive and negative configurations separately. From those statistics they derive an exact relation. The bias from dropping the sign equals a combination of two things: the gap between the groups' averages, and the average sign itself. The formula explains why pairing susceptibilities suffer most, and the authors offer it as a diagnostic for any simulation fighting the same problem.
arxiv-2512-04256:
Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Copilot have changed how software is learned as much as how it is written. Qiaolin Qin, Ronnie de Souza Santos, and Rodrigo Spinola survey that change in a 2025 software engineering education study. Their focus is the students: what benefits, challenges, and ethical worries shape undergraduate use.

The survey covered one hundred thirty undergraduates at two universities, mixing Likert-scale items with open-ended questions across five dimensions, from usage context to instructional expectations. Students reported using the tools mainly for incremental learning and advanced implementation, valuing brainstorming support and the confidence boost. They also reported unclear rationales from the tools and difficulty adapting outputs. Fairness and misconduct concerns stood out, alongside calls for clearer instructional guidance. The authors conclude that scaffolding, ethical policies, and adaptive teaching are needed so the tools support equitable learning.
arxiv-2512-04456:
Changjin Kim, HyeokJun Lee, and YoungJoon Yoo present GuidNoise, a tool that fakes realistic photo noise after seeing just one noisy-clean pair. Denoising tools learn best from real noise, but gathering paired real photos is slow and costly. Older noise fakers demand camera details and piles of paired shots. They also travel poorly between cameras. Their 2025 arXiv paper cuts those demands down to a single example pair.

GuidNoise guides a diffusion model with that one pair, drawn from the training set itself. A feature-shaping block makes the guide's noise style steer the output. A noise-aware loss refines the reverse process so fake noise matches real grain. The team reports strong results across camera settings the tool never saw. Cheap, faithful fake noise can widen training sets for phone cameras and medical scanners, where clean ground truth is scarce.
arxiv-2512-04756:
Mattia Piana and Stefano Tomasin design a way for a drone and a ground user to mint a shared secret key from the air itself, safe even from a curious insider. Physical-layer key generation turns channel randomness into keys that eavesdroppers cannot copy. Here the catch is the spy: another node inside the network, legitimately present yet curious. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the drone's freedom to move as the defense.

After a training phase, the drone, cast as Alice, picks a flight path of transmission spots. From each spot it sends to Bob on the ground, who estimates the channel gain. Those estimates seed the secret key. The spots are chosen to maximize a lower bound on key capacity over realistic Rician fading channels. Simulations confirm the scheme works. Moving transmitters could secure drone links in delivery, inspection, and emergency networks.
arxiv-2512-04856:
Kerim Dzhumageldyev, Filippo Airaldi, and Azita Dabiri present a safe learning framework that lets a predictive controller tune itself from data without breaking safety rules. Model predictive control plans actions over a horizon; control barrier functions certify that a system stays inside safe bounds. Marrying the two is powerful but touchy, since both sides carry parameters that are hard to set by hand. Their 2025 arXiv paper makes the whole controller the learning object.

The controller's parameters, including the barrier's shaping function, become weights that reinforcement learning adjusts from experience. Three variants differ in how the optimization is posed and how the shaping function is parameterized, one of them with a neural network. Numerical tests show policies that improve while respecting the safety certificate. Self-tuning safe controllers could serve robots, vehicles, and energy systems where hand tuning is costly and mistakes are dangerous.
arxiv-2512-04956:
Janette Suherli, Ivo Seitenzahl, Samar Safi-Harb, and co-authors settle the long-disputed distance to the Vela Junior supernova remnant. They do it by way of a young star's outflow. The remnant's size, age, and energy all hinge on its distance, which past estimates scattered widely. Using the MUSE spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope, the team found links between two gas clouds. One surrounds Vela Junior's central compact object. The other is the Herbig-Haro outflow of the nearby young star Ve 7-27. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues the two share one chemical home.

The star sits inside material thrown off by the massive star whose death made Vela Junior. The remnant's blast wave expands through the same medium. Gaia gives the star a firm distance, and the remnant inherits it. At the revised distance, the remnant spans a clear physical size, and its expansion speeds fall into place.
arxiv-2512-05056:
Junsong Cang, Yu Gao, and Yin-Zhe Ma forecast what a Moon-orbiting radio experiment could reveal about dark matter. If dark matter particles can bump into ordinary gas, the collisions would cool the early universe's hydrogen. They would also deepen the faint twenty-one-centimetre signal it left behind. That signal may explain an oddly deep absorption dip reported in 2018. The Hongmeng satellite will listen for that signal from lunar orbit, where Earthly interference is blocked.

The team simulates the data and fits it with models that vary the astrophysics and foreground haze together, so the forecast stays honest. The cautious plan observes only when both Earth and Sun hide behind the Moon. Even so, five years of data would tighten current limits on the dark matter collision strength by a large factor. A single month aloft would already improve on today's bounds several times over.
arxiv-2512-05456:
Stephen Salerno and five co-authors ask a question with a wink in its title and a warning in its answer: with prediction models everywhere, do scientists even need real data? Predicted values from pretrained algorithms increasingly substitute for measurements that are missing, expensive, or impossible to collect, as survey response falls and costs rise. The temptation is understandable — and dangerous, because inference quietly breaks when a guess stands in for the truth.

The authors characterize inference with predicted data. They show that every failure reduces to two classical culprits. One is bias, when predictions systematically shift what is being estimated or distort relationships. The other is variance, when the prediction model's uncertainty and the data's own variability are swept under the rug. High predictive accuracy, they stress, guarantees neither. They review corrective methods, root the framework in classical theory, and close with guidance for using predicted data with care.
arxiv-2512-05756: Gilles Blanchard, Nicolas Curien, Klara Krause, and Alexander Reisach study monotone paths in random graphs of the Erdős-Rényi kind. In this model the vertices are numbered. Edges appear at random, each with the same chance. Benjamini and Tzalik had found a phase transition for increasing paths in such graphs. The threshold sat at an edge chance near the logarithm of the vertex count, divided by that count. This paper sharpens the critical value with a smaller correction term. It also shows the transition window is very narrow.
arxiv-2512-05956:
Zheng-Duo Fan and Ashvin Vishwanath build the simplest useful model of a new high temperature superconductor, and design tests to expose how it works. The material, a layered nickel oxide, superconducts at temperatures that shocked the field, by a route distinct from the famous copper oxides and iron compounds. Several pairing mechanisms are on the table. The authors construct a minimal two band model that reproduces the Fermi surface shape seen in photoemission and in calculations.

Inside that model, they turn on two rival pairing mechanisms and compare what each predicts. The responses diverge sharply when a perpendicular electric field is applied: the field becomes a dial that separates the scenarios. Building on that split, the paper proposes three concrete experiments for the real material. Identifying the glue decides which theories survive.
arxiv-2512-06056:
Samer Seraj takes a piece of arithmetic folklore, the oddity that five divided by two gives two point five, digits rearranging themselves, and turns it into serious number theory. In any number base, one can ask when a division's digits relate to its inputs the same way. Seraj sets up the exponential Diophantine problem and attacks it. A modified Pythagorean parametrization nearly parametrizes all solutions.

All solutions with coprime numerator and denominator are found, and infinite families are constructed where the two are not coprime. A variant of Baker's theorem, from transcendental number theory, proves each base admits only finitely many solutions overall. Under the abc conjecture, fixed digit counts also allow only finitely many. A pattern a child could notice is pursued to deep conjectures.
arxiv-2512-06456:
Eric Ngondiep builds a faster, steadier way to simulate heat and radiation moving together through thick materials. The model is three dimensional and nonlinear, and the medium is anisotropic, meaning flow is easier in some directions than others. Such models serve in fields from furnace design to astrophysics, where radiation and conduction trade energy at every point.

His scheme pairs a mixed finite element method for the space part with a two stage treatment of the time part that first predicts, then corrects. That pairing keeps the time step under a stated limit, and under that limit he proves the method stable. Tests show the scheme is second order accurate in time and fourth order in space, matching the theory. The study casts the method as a practical tool that balances speed with accuracy for hard radiation problems.
arxiv-2512-06556:
Saeid Jamshidi and co authors warn that the instruction cards attached to AI tools can be poisoned. The Model Context Protocol lets language models call outside tools, guided by short descriptors that describe each tool. Current setups trust those cards blindly, even though they feed straight into the model's reasoning. An attacker who edits a card can steer which tool the model picks, a surface past defenses do not cover.

The team names three attack classes: poisoning a card, shadowing a real tool with a fake one, and a rug pull that swaps a good card for a bad one later. Their defense stacks checks: verify each card's integrity, vet its meaning with a helper model before it enters context, and guard at run time, without retraining. In trials, tampered cards drove unsafe tool calls in up to about a third of cases, and the full defense cut that sharply.
arxiv-2512-06756:
Abed Semre and Steven Frankel run a higher dimensional quantum algorithm on ordinary qubit hardware by faking the extra dimensions. Simon's problem is a classic where a quantum computer beats any classical one by an exponential margin. Its natural generalization uses qudits, units with more than two states, but real devices speak only qubits, the two state kind.

The authors define virtual qudits: patterns of qubits steered by controlled permutations and phase operations that act exactly like a qudit. With them they build a lifted oracle that hides the problem's secret shift in the higher dimension, using only qubit gates. They verify mathematically that the lifted circuit gives the right measurement statistics, and chart how circuit depth grows with dimension. Simulations in a standard quantum toolkit confirm example cases. The method offers a general bridge for porting qudit algorithms to today's machines.
arxiv-2512-06956:
Denis Belomestny and co-authors work on inverse reinforcement learning, the art of guessing what reward an expert is chasing by watching how the expert acts. A classic snag is that many different rewards can explain the same expert policy, so the answer is not unique. The team resolves the ambiguity by softening the model with entropy and rebuilding the reward from the mismatch in a soft Bellman equation, using least squares.

That combination singles out one well-defined reward that fits the expert. The expert's demonstrations are treated as a random walk whose steady pattern comes from the unknown policy. The policy itself is estimated by a penalized likelihood method over a family of action rules. The authors prove sharp bounds on how far the estimate can stray, and derive best-possible convergence rates for the rebuilt reward.
arxiv-2512-07756:
Mayank Anand, Ujair Alam, Surya Prakash, Priya Shukla, Gora Chand Nandi, and Domenec Puig wrote this 2025 medical imaging paper. Freehand ultrasound sweeps are hard to turn into clean three-dimensional volumes. Fast probe motion and flickering brightness introduce errors that erode clinical trust.

Their system, UltrasODM, assists the sonographer during the scan itself. A contrastive module groups frames that share similar motion. An optical-flow stream with Mamba temporal blocks estimates the probe's pose. A human-in-the-loop layer then judges each frame's uncertainty. Bayesian estimates and clinician-set thresholds drive that judgment call. Saliency maps show exactly which regions the system distrusts. When uncertainty crosses the line, gentle alerts suggest a fix. The operator can rescan a flagged region or slow the sweep down. On a clinical dataset, drift and distance errors fall against the prior system. Transparency, the authors argue, is what makes such assistance safe.
arxiv-2512-07956:
Oleksandr Tomalak, Qishan Liu, and Yu Feng Li, particle physicists, posted a detailed theory study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is inverse beta decay, the reaction by which detectors catch antineutrinos from nuclear reactors. As reactor experiments now aim for very fine precision on neutrino oscillation, the theory behind this reaction must match that accuracy.

The authors compute total and differential cross sections for the radiative form of the reaction, where a photon is also emitted. They use heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory and include radiative corrections, nucleon structure, weak magnetism, and recoil effects. New analytic formulas, a clear account of the collinear structure, and a full uncertainty analysis follow. The results support experiments such as JUNO and work on neutron decay.
arxiv-2512-08056:
The Belle II Collaboration, a large international team of particle physicists working in Japan, posted a measurement paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is a rare class of B meson decays in which the meson decays without producing a charm quark. Measuring how often these decays happen pins down a fundamental quantity, the size of the quark mixing element known as Vub.

The team uses collision data in which one B meson is fully reconstructed, letting them constrain the signal decay on the other side. A template fit separates the faint signal from a background of favored decays about fifty times larger. They measure partial branching fractions in several regions of phase space. The value of Vub they extract agrees with the world average from earlier inclusive measurements. Results like this test the internal consistency of the standard model of particle physics.
arxiv-2512-08156:
Mingbo Dou, Xu Chen, Zhiguo Liu, and colleagues, condensed matter physicists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is charge to spin conversion in altermagnets, a newer class of magnetic materials. Converting electric current into spin current is an efficient way to control magnetization with electricity, a goal for low power memory and logic devices.

The team proves that, in the nonrelativistic limit, the spin conductivity behind this conversion equals a difference of spin polarized conductivities. Using general spin group analysis, they derive formulas for how the conversion ratio changes with current direction, and find its maximum value. Calculations on representative altermagnets then show the effect in practice. The efficiency swings widely with direction, from zero up to several tens of percent. That strong direction dependence, they argue, gives device designers a new handle for generating spin currents without relativistic effects.
arxiv-2512-08556:
Ainna Yue Moreno Locubiche, Josep Vidal, Olga Munoz Medina, and Margarita Cabrera Bean, wireless engineers in Spain, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. In next generation mobile networks, a phone moving between cells must hand over cleanly, and too many handovers waste signaling and battery. The team combines three aids to make those decisions predictive instead of reactive.

A linear predictor forecasts signal power, so fading links are seen coming. Signal steering surfaces bounce signals around blockages. A learning agent, trained online, picks the target cell from context. Simulations under realistic conditions tested eight combinations. The learning agent and the prediction each cut handovers and ping pong switches. The surfaces improved link reliability.
arxiv-2512-08756:
Keshav Motwani and coauthors study how genes shape the link between brain structure and brain function. Scans can measure both anatomical connections between brain regions and their joint activity. Heritability work shows genes explain much of the person to person variation in each type of connectivity. But the genetic link between the two is hidden by unique life experience in observed data.

The authors build a regression framework for the latent genetic parts of structure and function. A core step is estimating genetic covariance for very high dimensional scan data, which older methods handle too slowly. Their constrained estimator is orders of magnitude faster with no loss of accuracy, and they pair it with regularized regression. On Human Connectome Project data, function is fairly predictable from structure at the genetic level, while it is barely predictable in raw observed data. That contrast suggests environment masks a strong genetic pattern.
arxiv-2512-08956:
Kumarjit Pathak and coauthors propose DW KNN, a transparent variant of the classic nearest neighbor classifier for machine learning. Standard distance weighted versions treat all chosen neighbors as equally reliable. In mixed feature spaces, that assumption hurts the reliability of predictions, since some neighbors may be noisy or mislabeled.

The new method combines exponential distance weighting with a measure of neighbor validity, which the authors call neighbor reliability. That pairing gives instance level interpretability, suppresses bad samples, and reduces sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. Evaluation on nine data sets shows solid average accuracy, ranking near the top among six methods and very close to the best ensemble variant. It also shows the lowest variation across validation folds, signaling stable predictions. Statistical tests confirm clear gains over two other weighted neighbor methods. The authors position it as a simple, effective option for high stakes uses that need explainable predictions.
arxiv-2512-09056:
Liming Kuang and coauthors present ConceptPose, a training free method to estimate the pose of objects. Pose estimation is fundamental for robotics and computer vision, yet most methods need extensive data set specific training. Large vision language models, by contrast, show strong zero shot skill, and the work bridges those two worlds.

ConceptPose uses a vision language model to build open vocabulary three dimensional concept maps. Each point in a map carries a concept vector derived from saliency maps. Robust correspondences between two such maps then allow precise estimation of relative pose. No object or data set specific training is used at any stage. On common zero shot relative pose benchmarks, the method reaches leading results and beats the strongest baseline by a large relative margin. That includes trained methods.
arxiv-2512-09256:
Ilija K. Nikolov leads a team probing hole-doped kagome superconductors, materials whose atoms form a woven lattice of triangles and hexagons. These compounds show an odd double-dome pattern of superconductivity as their chemistry is tuned. Chemical substitution also adds disorder, which has clouded the picture of how charge order and superconductivity interact.

The team used nuclear quadrupole resonance, a technique sensitive to local and static charge patterns, on a tin-substituted version of the kagome metal CsV3Sb5. They found patches of charge-density-wave order that stay frozen well above the usual transition temperature, pinned in place by defects. Tracking those patches with doping and temperature points to a hidden quantum critical point between the two superconducting domes, where the clean material's charge order would vanish. Doping breaks the order into fragments, while disorder helps the patches survive.
arxiv-2512-09356:
Yunhao Wang and colleagues present NOC4SC, a framework for semantic communication among many users sharing the same airwaves. Wireless networks face surging numbers of connected devices, and interference between users threatens service quality. Semantic communication sends meaning rather than raw bits, but multi-user versions still need to keep users' signals apart.

NOC4SC lets users transmit at the same time on the same frequency without spectrum spreading, using non-orthogonal codewords. A Swin Transformer encoder-decoder, shared across users, extracts each user's semantic features, and the design keeps one user's data from being decoded by others. An adaptive block adjusts to channel noise and shapes the features to be nearly orthogonal, reducing interference. In experiments, the framework matched a leading multi-user semantic system and beat other baselines. The authors present it as a bandwidth-efficient design for interference-heavy networks.
arxiv-2512-09456:
Ronen Shekel, Ohad Lib, Sébastien M. Popoff, and Yaron Bromberg show that pairs of entangled photons can keep their spatial pattern stable across a wide range of colors, even after passing through messy materials. When light crosses a complex medium, its output pattern normally changes rapidly with wavelength, which limits the useful bandwidth of imaging and communication methods.

The pairs they study are hyper-entangled, linked in both space and spectrum at once. Because the two photons' colors are anti-correlated, the color-dependent scrambling one photon suffers is canceled to first order by its twin. The team demonstrates this analytically and numerically, and defines a two-photon bandwidth that can far exceed the classical one. They illustrate the cancellation in multimode fibers, thin diffusers, and blazed gratings, and show it enables broadband shaping of quantum light wavefronts, with uses in quantum imaging, communication, and sensing.
arxiv-2512-09556:
Felix Sainsbury-Martinez, Greg Cooke, and Catherine Walsh simulate what icy comet impacts do to the atmospheres of planets, focusing on how much atmosphere escapes. On Earth, water vapor carries hydrogen upward, but a cold trap in the lower atmosphere freezes most of it out, limiting hydrogen escape. On a tidally locked planet, one side always faces its star, and the day-night contrast drives circulation that might slip water past such a trap.

Coupling comet and atmosphere models, they compare tidally locked and Earth-like atmospheres, with and without impacts. Unimpacted, the tidally locked world lost hydrogen at rates similar to Earth's, despite being cooler and drier near the surface. Impacts made the difference dramatic: a day-side impact produced escape rates about ten times higher than a night-side impact on the same planet. The authors stress that the circulation pattern decides how processes play out.
arxiv-2512-09956:
Emily Clader and Vanessa Jelmyer explain a neat pattern linking music theory to pure mathematics. A Pythagorean scale encodes pitches as ratios built from powers of three over powers of two. The two step property measures how evenly spaced such a scale is. Roughly, its notes should use only two sizes of step. The authors give a mathematician's account of exactly which Pythagorean scales have this property. The resulting list is striking: it contains the five note, seven note, and twelve note scales.

Those are the pentatonic, diatonic, and chromatic scales of music theory. The authors state openly that the results are not new. After posting, they learned the characterization already existed in work by Carey and Clampitt and others in music theory. They keep the preprint public anyway, because it is written for mathematicians with no musical background.
arxiv-2512-10056:
Alireza Namazi, Amirreza Dolatpour Fathkouhi, and Heman Shakeri attack a failure mode of medical forecasting called exposure bias. Autoregressive models predict the next value from their own past predictions. Trained with teacher forcing, where true past values are always supplied, they become unstable over long horizons in closed loop control. Their method, Soft-Token Trajectory Forecasting, propagates whole probability distributions instead of single point guesses, soft tokens that keep uncertainty alive through the forecast.

A risk aware decoding step then chooses trajectories that minimize expected clinical harm, not just average error. In glucose forecasting, average zone based risk fell by about eighteen percent. In blood pressure forecasting, effective clinical risk dropped by roughly fifteen percent. The work supports learned forecasters inside real predictive control loops.
arxiv-2512-10156:
Jan Kemper and Davud Rostam-Afschar propose a test statistic for adaptive experiments, where treatment assignments change as results come in. Adaptive designs are spreading through economics and practice because they learn while they run. The catch is inference: data gathered adaptively break the assumptions behind standard causal tests. Their statistic, batched ordinary least squares, fits the common design where adaptation happens in batches. It pools the treatment control difference from each period, weighting periods so their precision is matched even when noise differs across periods.

The combined statistic is a scaled average of per period adjusted differences. From it, valid confidence intervals follow in large samples. Tests check rejection rates in the realistic regime: few treatment periods, with few or many observations in each batch.
arxiv-2512-10556: Minoru Wakimoto studies admissible modules of the affine Lie algebra of type C2 at integer level, concentrating on the non-principal and non-coprincipal cases that sit outside the best-understood families. He follows these modules through quantum Hamiltonian reduction, a standard way of producing smaller, related representations. And proves that the resulting characters enjoy modular invariance under the congruence subgroup of level two. The note adds these overlooked module families to the list of cases where the modular symmetry is confirmed.
arxiv-2512-10656:
Léa Bohbot and co-authors ask how fast attention becomes itself. As language model context windows stretch, attention is computed over more tokens. And the authors define token sample complexity: the rate at which attention over a finite set of tokens converges to its infinite-token limit. That rate decides how much of a long context the mechanism is using.

For token distributions that are compactly supported or sub-Gaussian, the attention map converges uniformly at a rate set by the square root of the token count. But the constant grows exponentially with radius, making the bound useless for long contexts. A second result tracks the moments of the distribution, with a constant that grows only polynomially and an exponent shaped by attention geometry and the token spectrum. In the hard-attention limit the rate turns logarithmic. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirmed the slowdown, including in accuracy.
arxiv-2512-10756:
Zijian Wu and a large team build a verifier that can check long chains of thought without bankrupting the annotation budget. Outcome-based verifiers only see a model's final answer and miss rotten steps in the middle, while process verifiers need step labels that are too expensive to collect at scale. Their outcome-based process verifier threads the needle by checking the reasoning behind summarised outcomes.

Training runs as an active learning loop: the current best verifier flags its most uncertain cases, experts annotate just those. And rejection fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards train the next round. On the team's OPV-Bench the verifier set a new state of the art, beating much larger open models, and it flagged false positives in synthetic data much as experts did. Paired with policy models, it lifted reasoning accuracy as compute grew.
arxiv-2512-10956:
Wentao Zhou and colleagues present a robot navigation model built for busy city streets, where people and vehicles move in unstructured ways. Most systems map a single camera view straight to actions and hope that understanding of space and motion will emerge on its own. That learning needs huge amounts of labelled action data that are hard to collect.

Their model, Stereo4DWalker in the arXiv record, uses stereo input and builds explicit structures for geometry and motion over time. Those structures feed a navigation transformer through special attention layers. Training used a large dataset drawn from internet stereo videos with automatically labelled actions. The system beat prior methods while using only a small fraction of their training data.
arxiv-2512-11256:
Mario Villanueva and fellow authors build feedback controllers for non-linear systems with explicit guarantees, using a convex form of Lyapunov function. Many engineered systems are non-linear and discrete in time, and controllers must stay robust while keeping testing fast and memory predictable. Their method starts from the value function of a worst case, long horizon control problem.

They approximate that value function with a piecewise affine function whose shape is constrained by a chosen template. Enforcing the approximation to act as a generalised control Lyapunov function preserves robustness and results guarantees. The payoff is an explicit controller whose storage size and testing time are set in advance by the template. A case study on the constrained Van der Pol oscillator, a classic non-linear benchmark, produced a certified controller over a large operating region.
arxiv-2512-11356:
Meng-Li Shih, Ying-Huan Chen, Yu-Lun Liu, and Brian Curless rebuild moving scenes in three dimensions from a single casual video, without designing a new scene representation. Dynamic Gaussian splatting renders such scenes well, but its quality hinges on the guiding information fed in beforehand. Casual phone footage gives weak depth, shaky object masks, and unreliable motion tracks.

Their fully automatic pipeline sharpens those priors instead. Segmentation combined with geometric error maps yields masks that follow thin structures closely. Those masks improve depth through an object level loss and support skeleton based sampling plus re identification for complete two dimensional tracks. Two further objectives use virtual views to delete floating artefacts and tie motion nodes to the tracks, preserving fine geometry and coherent movement. The system surpasses earlier methods for monocular dynamic reconstruction and renders visibly better results.
arxiv-2512-11556:
Stefan Hägele and fellow authors classify objects hidden behind packaging using millimetre wave radar that can see through thin materials. Such radar suits industrial and robotic perception because it works in adverse settings where cameras struggle. Earlier work with multiple antenna radar had shown occluded objects inside cardboard could be recognised, but accuracy left room to grow and other frequency bands were untested.

Their ACCOR method processes the complex valued radar signal with a complex valued convolutional backbone. It adds a multi head attention layer. Training uses a hybrid loss mixing normal classification with a guided contrastive term that pulls same class cases jointly. They extended an current data set at one frequency with a new subset at a slightly higher frequency. Accuracy beat prior radar specific and adapted image models on both bands, supporting the combination of complex valued learning, attention, and contrast for hidden object spotting.
arxiv-2512-11756:
Valeria Díaz Moreno and co-authors check whether quiet neighbor qubits spoil a key quantum gate in fluxonium circuits. Fluxonium qubits are prized for clean control, and clean two qubit gates exist for pairs. Bigger chips, though, park idle spectator qubits next to the working pair.

The team models four linked fluxonium qubits and runs the CNOT gate on two of them. Errors from spectators shrink fast when their tones sit far from the working pair tones. With the right tone layout, gate errors fell below one in ten thousand, with gates under 100 nanoseconds. Since links are local, the same layout rules should scale to long chains, a hopeful sign for bigger machines.
arxiv-2512-12856:
Saad Alqithami looks at how AI agents that talk with people over long periods should handle memory. Storing everything is costly and raises privacy risks. Forgetting too much, by contrast, makes an agent lose track of goals and people.

He presents MaRS, a memory plan inspired by human cognition, with typed records for events, facts, social ties, and tasks. Six forgetting rules balance recall, privacy, and cost. A test suite called FiFA checks agents on story sense, goals, social recall, privacy, and cost. Across 300 test runs, a hybrid forgetting rule scored 0.911 overall, the best result reported.
arxiv-2512-13156:
Viktoria Freingruber and co-authors present a new model of microbial aggregates, clumps where several bacterial species live and grow together. Inside a clump, species compete for shared food, and some benefit from the waste products of others. Space matters as much as chemistry here.

Their model uses partial differential equations with cross-diffusion and reaction terms. Bacteria spread passively, pushed by population pressure, and grow as food allows. Numerical tests show the model reproduces the key spatial patterns seen in earlier individual based simulations across three check scenarios. They also derive a competition system from a biased random walk on a lattice.
arxiv-2512-13256:
Bilal Kousar and co-authors report steady, reproducible quantized transport in a graphene quantum Hall system, a platform whose quirks have limited its use in topological superconductivity. Screening long-range interactions with a metallic bismuth selenide back gate stabilized the effect at low magnetic fields.

Beyond resistance plateaus, they built gate-defined junctions between chiral and helical channels that can pass or block a single helical channel on demand. That control is not possible in standard time-reversal symmetric systems. They traced quantization breakdown to contact induced doping and fixed it with large area contacts. The system suits future topological devices that need superconducting proximity.
arxiv-2512-13956:
Zishan Bai and co-authors present AOI, a multi-agent framework for autonomous IT operations in cloud-native systems. Incidents unfold across microservices while logs and metrics flood in faster than operators can read them. Recovery actions must be coordinated without losing the causal context that makes them safe.

AOI splits duties across an Observer, a read-only Probe, and a guarded Executor, linked by dynamic scheduling. A hierarchical memory system with LLM-based compression preserves context across long incidents. In AIOpsLab simulations and Loghub-derived scenarios, AOI raised task success to 94.2% and cut mean time to resolution by 34.4% versus the strongest baseline. It compressed context by 72.4% while keeping 92.8% of diagnostic information.
arxiv-2512-14356:
Dominik Pacholski, Sandro Mereghetti, and Martin Topinka present a catalog of magnetar bursts from the INTEGRAL satellite in a 2025 paper. Magnetars are young neutron stars powered mainly by magnetic energy, and they emit short bursts of hard X rays lasting under a second.

The team searched more than twenty years of archival data from the IBIS instrument, covering 15 keV to 1 MeV. They found 1349 bursts from 21 of the 34 magnetars and candidates examined. Burst durations follow a lognormal distribution centered near 0.1 seconds. Most bursts came from three very active sources. Their spectra fit an exponentially cut off power law, with peak energies mostly between about 20 and 100 keV, depending on the source.
arxiv-2512-15256:
Hoang-Anh Le and two coauthors argue that entanglement between fractional charges can draw a curved space into being. Some topologically ordered materials host anyons, particles with fractional charge and exotic statistics. The authors study pairs of half charged semions that arise on opposite zigzag edges of a disordered graphene nanoribbon.

Though far apart, the pair shows long range quantum entanglement. The team analyzes how that entanglement scales, using mutual information, and embeds the ribbon into a bulk geometry like anti de Sitter space. In that picture, the entanglement defines minimal surfaces in the bulk, giving a geometric view of the edge correlations. The result is a holographic portrait of fractionalized degrees of freedom in a nearly one dimensional system. It shows emergent geometry from entanglement even without conformal symmetry.
arxiv-2512-15656:
Pavel Sekatski and Jef Pauwels show that all entangled states are nonlocal in the broadcast scenario in a 2025 paper. Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are not the same: some entangled states admit a local hidden variable model for all local measurements. That gap has stood as a basic fact of quantum theory.

In a minimal broadcast extension of the Bell setup, the gap disappears. For every entangled state, the authors find local broadcasting maps and measurements whose four party correlations no separable source across the main cut can reproduce. They also show all multipartite states, mixed ones included, can be broadcast self tested under a natural operational definition.
arxiv-2512-15756:
Yoon Pyo Lee and co authors show that scientific feedback can push generative models beyond the conventions in their training data in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Human design habits narrow the options present in training sets, and models learn those narrowed preferences. Feedback tied to real performance might reopen the search.

Tests cover reactor lattice design with simulated feedback and chemical reaction choices with measured yields. In both, adaptation improved performance while raising the share of choices that training data had excluded. In the reaction case, use of excluded ligands rose from 0.29 to about 0.70 as yield error fell. Controls link the shift to the scientific objective itself.
arxiv-2512-16156:
L Levin leads a large SKA working group team in surveying neutron stars in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. More than 3,500 non-accreting neutron stars are known, from ordinary pulsars to magnetars with extreme magnetic fields. The SKA telescopes should swell that census, adding radio pulsars to every branch of the family and likely revealing new kinds of sources.

The authors review the types of neutron stars and the questions a bigger sample can answer. Open puzzles include how isolated pulsars evolve, how magnetars connect to high-field and long-period pulsars, and what dense matter inside these stars is made of. More pulsars in binaries and triples would sharpen tests of gravity and general relativity. The paper maps how SKA sensitivity, wide views, and many beams enable that research.
arxiv-2512-16256:
Rahul Thakur and three co-authors test modified gravity in their 2025 arXiv paper. They study f(R, phi) theories in the Palatini formalism, where curvature and a scalar field jointly drive cosmic expansion. The goal is one model that covers both the early inflation era and today's accelerating universe.

Assuming the curvature part behaves like Starobinsky gravity, they check stability after inflation and find two fixed points that give a stable, accelerating late universe. Data from the DESI survey, cosmic chronometers, and supernovae tighten the picture further. One surviving fixed point has expansion driven by a phantom scalar field, which acts more strongly than a cosmological constant. Timescale arguments suggest that point may be temporary, with the universe later settling into potential-driven expansion.
arxiv-2512-16456:
Masashi Hatano and five co-authors synthesize human movement in an arXiv paper published in 2025. Before picking something up, people spot the target from afar, a behavior called gaze priming, then approach and reach. Generating realistic motion with that two-stage pattern is the paper's focus.

The team curated 23,700 gaze-primed reaching sequences from five public data sets, the first collection of its kind. They pretrained a text-conditioned diffusion model for motion, then fine-tuned it on goal poses and target locations from those sequences. A new metric, Prime Success, joins Reach Success in judging whether generated motion truly imitates the natural pattern. Across all five data sets, the model produced varied full-body motion showing both priming and reaching, beating baselines and recent methods. Such synthesis supports animation, robotics, and virtual character control.
arxiv-2512-16856:
Nenad Tomašev and coauthors argue that AI safety must cover groups of agents, not just single systems. Most safety work assumes one monolithic general AI, yet capability may first arrive as patchwork teams of lesser agents with split skills that coordinate.

With tool-using agents now deployed and able to talk and team up, the authors call this an urgent gap. Their frame for distributional AGI safety centers on virtual agent sandbox economies, markets whose rules are sealed or semi-sealed. Agent trades there would run under robust market rules with audits, reputation tracking, and oversight, aiming to curb joint risks that single-agent checks cannot see.
arxiv-2512-16956:
Shravan Chaudhari and coauthors present SpIDER. It is a retrieval method that helps coding agents find the right functions in a large codebase. The query may be a bug report or a request. Sparse word matching ignores the graph shape of code. Dense embedding search ignores it too. That shape holds the calls and containment links.

SpIDER grows its candidate set along that graph. It tags each added function with the seed and link type that brought it in. The set thus stays auditable at a fixed budget. The graph is built from syntax trees on demand. On SpIDER-Bench, recall at 20 rose by at least 13 percent relative on containment links. It rose by at least 27 percent once call links were added. The bench draws on three SWE benchmarks across four languages.
arxiv-2512-17256:
Shakir Ali and three co-authors build special matrices used to scramble data inside ciphers. An MDS matrix spreads each input across many outputs, which makes coded messages harder to untangle. Recursive kinds are prized because they can be built step by step on cheap hardware. The team works over Galois rings, number systems richer than plain fields.

Their recipes grow out of skew polynomials, where the order of terms matters. They prove rules that tell which polynomials yield good matrices, plus one rule based on the roots of a linked polynomial. The methods widen the known family a great deal, even in the non-commutative setting. The binary case used in real ciphers gets special attention as a target for fast diffusion layers.
arxiv-2512-17556:
L. Lafforgue and coauthors based in Innsbruck probe how bosonic erbium atoms in mixed spin states scatter off one another. Tuning the atoms near resonances reveals how their collisions can be turned up, down, or nearly off.

The team reports scattering resonances between and within spin states that have an asymmetric shape and a clear dip in atom loss. A simplified model with several coupled channels traces the shape to destructive interference between pathways, the classic Fano effect. A whole series of these Fano Feshbach resonances across the spin channels ties back to one molecular state. Such control over collisions is a basic tool for building quantum matter from ultracold atoms with many internal states.
arxiv-2512-17856:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a hunt for heavy new particles that decay into a top quark and its antimatter twin. The search uses 140 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 TeV from the Large Hadron Collider. Chosen events hold one or two light particles called leptons, missing energy, and at least two jets.

Targets span masses from 0.4 to 5.0 TeV and cover three guessed particle types, from new force carriers to gravity related states. The counts matched what the Standard Model predicts, so no new particle showed up. Instead the team sets firm caps on how often such particles could be made, which narrows the space for future hunts.
arxiv-2512-17956:
Victor Stasiu presents a small toolkit for checking how chatbots state their confidence and handle ranking tasks. Safety tuning can make leading models hedge or refuse too often, which hurts teamwork. His Victor Calibration method asks a model to recheck its own evidence in several passes and report a rising or falling confidence score.

Two companion checks audit model behavior without claims about inner feelings, and stress test whether rankings stay stable and fair. Trials on several Claude models showed smooth confidence paths and no broken safety rules. Stasiu is clear that one person ran the work, with one session per model, so the results are early hints that others should test.
arxiv-2512-18056:
Daniel David builds probabilistic digital twins of people, not machines. Apps often sum up a user with one fixed vector of numbers, which hides doubt and meaning. His twin treats each user as a hidden random state that gives rise to the answers and clicks we see.

A variational autoencoder learns those states from a survey style data set, keeping the math fully about chance rather than fixed traits. A checking pipeline then ties each hidden axis to real behavior with plain statistical tests. Axes lined up with traits like opinion strength and decisiveness. Most user differences formed smooth ranges, not tight clusters, which favors soft, doubt aware profiles.
arxiv-2512-18456:
Qilong Wu and three co-authors survey the security of AI-for-code systems, the tools like GitHub Copilot that now write, translate, and check software. Their systematization paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, covers three core uses and finds the same gaps recurring. Benchmarks lean on Python and toy problems, standard security datasets are missing, test data leaks into training, and defenses against attacks stay fragile.

A comparison of six leading models shows the problems in practice. Insecure patterns persist in generated code, and flaw detection breaks under attacks that preserve meaning. Fine-tuning can pull security goals off course, and translation gives uneven gains. The authors chart three fixes: secure defaults in generation, stronger detection benchmarks, and translation into safer languages.
arxiv-2512-20056:
Hao Li leads a nine-author team locating disaster photos on the map when seconds count. Cross-view geolocalization matches a ground photo against satellite views. It estimates where the shot was taken. ProbGLC reworks that task for disaster response. The events span hurricanes, wildfires, floods, and tornadoes. The frame joins probabilistic and fixed-output models in one. It does not make the user pick between them.

The probabilistic side gives uncertainty. It yields full distributions over places, plus a localizability score for each scene. That score says how findable the scene is. It backs clear choices on where to send resources. Tests ran on two cross-view disaster data sets. Accuracy sat near the top at both one-kilometer and twenty-five-kilometer tolerances. Data and code are public.
arxiv-2512-20856:
NVIDIA introduces the Nemotron 3 family, three open language models named Nano, Super, and Ultra. All share a hybrid Mamba-Transformer design with mixture-of-experts layers, built for agent tasks, reasoning, and conversation. Context windows reach one million tokens across the family.

Super and Ultra add two refinements: training in a compact four-bit format and a LatentMoE method said to raise quality, plus prediction layers that speed up text generation. Post-training used reinforcement learning in many environments, teaching tool use and adjustable reasoning budgets. Nano ships first with open weights; the larger two were announced to follow. NVIDIA pledges weights, software, recipes, and releasable data.
arxiv-2512-20956:
Xianjin Yang, Houman Owhadi, and four co-authors teach a machine-learning method to solve equations whose unknowns are entire functions. Functional renormalization group equations track how a physical theory changes across scales and are notoriously hard beyond perturbation theory. Their framework uses Gaussian process operator learning, building the representation directly on function space so it depends on no particular equation or grid.

Physical knowledge can enter through the prior mean or the kernel design, keeping the solver honest where data is thin. On the Wetterich and Wilson-Polchinski equations the method matches or beats the standard local-potential approximation while remaining far more flexible. Because it handles non-constant fields, it opens a route to configurations such as instantons that cruder approximations cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-21156:
Kiyoshi Sogo exhibits a three-way mirror in classical analysis. Many quantities can be written simultaneously as an infinite product, an infinite series, and a continued fraction. Three languages say one thing. He calls such an identity a triplicity. The point is computational. When the three forms agree, whichever is easiest to evaluate hands you the value of the others. That includes series that resist direct summation.

Triplicity reaches even divergent series, assigning them definite sums. Among the examples stands a ferociously divergent alternating series recorded in Entry 7 of Gauss's diary. Its terms explode through powers of two. The method obtains a finite value for it, about 0.4275 and then further digits beyond. Analysts fond of Ramanujan-style identities gain a unifying frame: products, sums, and fractions are not three toolboxes but one, and even divergence can be negotiated with rather than merely feared.
arxiv-2512-21256:
Alaa Alburai, Lluis Galbany, and twenty co-authors profile the dim cousins of cosmology's standard candles. From the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release, 3,628 Type Ia supernovae, they extract 124 subluminous events, the largest single-instrument sample of its kind. The split runs 87 of the 91bg-like subtype, a dozen 86G-like, 18 04gs-like, and 7 02es-like explosions. Template fits, velocity and line-strength measurements, and averaged spectra per subtype anchor the picture.

Nearly all subluminous events prove intrinsically red, not merely dust-dimmed. Standard light-curve fitters, never trained on such objects, compensate by distorting their color parameters. The explosions favor massive, red host galaxies and the reddest local environments, with two subtypes erupting unusually far from their galactic centers. Two spectral diagnostics, a blended absorption strength near 4300 angstroms and a color-stretch measure, suffice to subclassify them, giving surveys a cheap sorting key for these faint but informative deaths.
arxiv-2512-21456:
Sukanya Krishna, Marie-Laure Charpignon, and Maimuna Majumder compare ways of estimating excess deaths from substance overdose in the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic. Excess mortality means deaths beyond what pre-pandemic patterns would predict. Getting this count right matters for judging the pandemic's toll.

The authors train models on national CDC data from 2015 to 2019 and project forward through 2023. They test the traditional SARIMA method against three deep learning designs: LSTM, Seq2Seq, and Transformer networks. The LSTM gives the best point estimates and the best-calibrated uncertainty ranges. Attention-based models do worse, apparently because they overfit historical averages instead of following new trends. The team also releases an open pipeline with prediction intervals, ready for state health departments. Their conclusion is that carefully validated neural models can beat classical statistics for public health forecasting under sudden change.
arxiv-2512-21656:
Yingying Yu, Chungang Zhu, and their co-authors tackle a reliability problem in 3D modeling: Coons volume mappings can fold over themselves. A Coons volume fills a solid by interpolating between its boundary surfaces, and it is widely used to generate meshes. If its Jacobian determinant touches zero or goes negative, the mapping is no longer regular and later work turns unstable.

The authors build a check with three parts. First, a general sufficient condition works for any boundary parameterization. For Bézier-form volumes, a second test reduces the check to the positivity of control coefficients of the Jacobian. A third, necessary condition, built from subdivision and Bézier blossoming, guarantees regularity in every subdomain. Together these yield an algorithm the team validates numerically. Regularity tracks how alike the two boundary surfaces are. Tests are fast, and the method extends to multi-patch B-spline volumes.
arxiv-2512-22056:
MaxCut, an NP-hard graph problem, tempts quantum methods, but such algorithms hit barren plateaus and hardware limits at scale. Yuefeng Lin and colleagues extend their distributed variational quantum eigensolver with a hybrid perturbation strategy, solving weighted MaxCut problems of up to one thousand vertices with only ten qubits.

Results show the method beats the classical Goemans-Williamson algorithm, and warm-starting from that algorithm's solutions improves them further. As a test, the team applied the solver to phasing on sequencing data for the human ABCA1 gene, producing haplotypes rivaling a projected classical run. It is NISQ-compatible and scalable for near-term quantum-enhanced optimization.
arxiv-2512-22156:
Jin Sob Kim, Hyun Joon Park, Wooseok Shin, and Sung Won Han describe their entry to a sound event localization and detection challenge run under DCASE 2022. The task asks systems to spot sounds in recordings, name their class, and estimate where each sound came from. The team built a ResNet-based model inside a system designed to survive messy real-world audio.

Their recipe leans on heavy data augmentation and a training mix that blends real sound scenes with simulated ones while keeping enough real samples in every batch. External sound sources add further variety. At test time they apply augmentation again and ensemble models by clustering confident predictions. The system beat the challenge baselines and stayed competitive on real recordings.
arxiv-2512-22356:
Ella M. Mansfield, Delaney A. Dunne, and Dongwoo T. Chung sharpen a technique for finding faint cosmic signals by stacking. Line-intensity mapping charts the universe at low resolution through spectral line glow, and stacking co-adds small map cutouts at known emitter positions to lift signal out of noise. Their upgrade fits an assumed signal shape rather than simply averaging, in two spatial dimensions or in three including the spectral axis.

They also stack at source coordinates more precise than the map's resolution. Tested on simulations mimicking the COMAP Pathfinder, the fitting methods gained up to twenty-five percent in detection significance over the plain stack. The best profile was wider than the telescope beam and Lorentzian in frequency. Clustering effects, including fingers-of-God smearing, shape what works best.
arxiv-2512-22656:
Argha Kamal Samanta, Deepak Mewada, Monalisa Sarma, and Debasis Samanta benchmark machine learning for reading brain-wave recordings across many disorders at once. Clinical EEG reading is manual, slow, and variable, and most automated work targets single problems like seizure spotting. This study instead classifies eleven brain disorders, from time-critical acute conditions to chronic childhood disorders and conditions with only faint EEG signs.

Recordings were processed in a standard bipolar montage and summed up by features spanning time statistics, spectra, complexity, and channel links. With severe class imbalance, the team tuned decision thresholds explicitly for sensitivity. Recall exceeded eighty percent for most kinds, and calibration lifted recall for rare conditions by fifteen to thirty points. Important features matched known clinical EEG markers.
arxiv-2512-22756:
K. S. Babu, Rahool Kumar Barman, and Dorival Gonçalves study whether the Large Hadron Collider could see lepton number violated by two units, a striking signal tied to how neutrinos get their mass. Their setting is the leptoquark version of the Zee model, where Majorana neutrino masses are generated in a loop of particles that includes leptoquarks, hypothetical particles linking quarks and leptons.

Those leptoquark interactions can produce two same-sign leptons plus jets in proton collisions, a signature with few ordinary backgrounds. After applying current experimental limits, the authors identify the main production channels and run a detailed collider analysis. They find the high-luminosity LHC could probe leptoquark masses up to about one and a half trillion electron volts in mass units. Seeing such a signal would directly confirm lepton number violation and prove neutrinos are Majorana particles.
arxiv-2512-22856:
Matthaus Zering, Jolyon Joyce, Tal Gurfinkel, and Jingbo Wang compare two remedies for a known weakness of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. That quantum algorithm is a favorite candidate for beating classical optimization, but random starting parameters usually make its gradients vanish, so training stalls. One remedy pretrains parameters with a Lie-algebraic classical simulation; the other, called NV-QWOA, restricts the search to a small subspace steered by only three hyperparameters.

The test bed is the unweighted MaxCut problem at deep circuit depth, run across hundreds of random and regular graphs with sixteen vertices each. Both strategies beat randomly initialized runs by a wide margin. NV-QWOA reached a mean approximation ratio close to ninety-nine percent within sixty iterations, while the pretrained approach improved more slowly over five hundred iterations. The authors read this as evidence that a well-structured small parameter space trains more robustly than pretraining.
arxiv-2512-23156:
Ivan Gonoskov, Christian Hünecke, and Stefanie Gräfe explain how laser-driven matter can emit light with quantum, nonclassical properties. Their focus is high-order harmonic generation, where an intense laser makes atoms radiate at many times the driving frequency. Starting from a Pauli-Fierz model of coupled light and matter, they split the joint wavefunction into a field-driven electronic state and a quantized light mode obeying coupled equations.

Inside that framework, nonclassicality has a simple dial: the bend in the electronic dipole's response to the light mode's coordinate. A nearly constant dipole yields coherent radiation. A linear response produces squeezed light. Stronger bends generate Wigner-function negativity, a stronger signature of quantumness. The mechanism is shown on atomic and molecular models, and its scaling with many emitters is checked. The authors present the picture as a design basis for engineering quantum light in intense laser-matter settings.
arxiv-2512-23356:
Xin Zhang and co-authors propose SGR, a framework that steadies large language model reasoning by grounding each step in a knowledge graph. Models answering complex questions often absorb noisy or irrelevant material during generation and drift into confident errors. SGR's response is to build a small external subgraph tailored to the query, pulling relevant entities and relations from a knowledge base before the model starts reasoning.

The model then works through the problem step by step over that structured subgraph, rather than free-associating over raw text. Several reasoning paths are generated and finally integrated into one answer. Across multiple benchmark datasets, the framework consistently beat strong baselines, which the authors attribute to the subgraph filtering out noise and giving each inference step explicit factual footing. The work is aimed at question answering and other tasks where deep, verifiable logical inference matters more than fluency.
arxiv-2512-23456:
Sukanya Mitra studies relativistic hydrodynamics, the theory that describes hot, fast-moving fluids such as the matter formed in heavy-ion collisions. Working from the relativistic kinetic equation, she uses a proposed collision kernel built to conserve both energy-momentum and particle current exactly. The paper appeared in a version accepted by Physics Letters B.

Mitra analyzes the poles of the kinetic equation and the dispersion relations that follow from them. In the long-wavelength limit these relations show the gradient structure expected of hydrodynamics, with spatial and time gradients appearing together in a single relaxation operator. She argues that keeping this structure, including time derivatives, is what protects the theory from breaking causality at any truncation order. The paper runs to just seven pages.
arxiv-2512-23556:
Xiaolin Zhang and five co-authors assess how well proposed Moon-based gravitational-wave detectors could locate sources on the sky. A lunar interferometer would fill the frequency gap between space missions such as LISA and TianQin and detectors on Earth. The team studies CIGO, a planned observatory on the rim of a lunar crater near the north pole, using the Fisher-matrix method for steady sources in the decihertz band.

Above a tenth of a hertz, CIGO localized sources better than LISA or TianQin and dominated a combined network. That holds provided lunar noise can be controlled at low frequencies. An upgraded design adding a fourth station at the crater floor, forming a tetrahedron, improved angular resolution about fivefold and widened sky coverage across the target band.
arxiv-2512-23756:
Pierre Mackenzie surveys and tests sparse random projections, a dimensionality reduction tool with a famous guarantee behind it. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss theorem says a cloud of points in a high-dimensional space can be mapped into far fewer dimensions while nearly preserving all pairwise distances. The classical construction multiplies by a dense Gaussian random matrix, which is slow when data are huge.

Sparse random matrices, with most entries zero, multiply much faster and are preferred in applications. Mackenzie outlines the constructions and proofs of Achlioptas and of Kane and Nelson, the contemporary standard, and then implements the sparse constructions to compare them empirically against the standard Gaussian version. The paper reads as a guided tour from theorem to practice, showing what sparsity costs and what it buys.
arxiv-2512-24056:
Wenye Li, Hongxu Chen, Jiacai Liu, and Ke Wei analyze policy mirror descent. The method is a general framework in reinforcement learning. Many policy gradient methods are special cases of it. The open question is sample complexity. How much data does the method need? Here samples arrive as one Markovian stream. Values are learned on the fly by temporal difference updates.

Earlier analyses assumed a simulator with free restarts. Others assumed values precomputed to a set accuracy. This paper studies two variants that learn values alongside the policy. One is off-policy. The other is mixed. With a small fixed step size, near-optimal performance is proven. The sample count scales like one over the squared error target. Adaptive step sizes remove a leftover logarithmic factor. The results tighten expectations for online data.
arxiv-2512-24156:
Evgenii Rudakov, Jonathan Shock, and Benjamin Ultan Cowley take on ARC-AGI-3. The benchmark holds game-like tasks. An agent must infer the rules by playing. Feedback is sparse, and levels grow harder. Leading language models fail these tasks badly. The authors try the opposite of learning. They use careful, systematic exploration tracked in a graph.

The agent breaks each frame into visual parts. Possible actions are ranked by visual salience. Explored states and transitions form a directed graph. The agent remembers what has been tried. It steers toward untested state-action pairs by the shortest path. On the preview challenge, it solved a median of thirty levels. That was out of fifty-two levels across six games. It placed third on the private leaderboard. The code is open source.
arxiv-2512-24256:
Dominic Batzler and five colleagues measure tritium sticking to fusion materials. Tritium adsorbs on surfaces and causes problems. Fusion plants and tritium laboratories both face them. How much accumulates depends on the material. Contaminated surfaces then need cleaning, preferably in place. Ozone under ultraviolet light is one candidate method.

A single setup at Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe addresses both questions. Samples meet gaseous tritium while activity is tracked over time. The chamber can then fill with dry air, plain or ozonated. Beryllium and tungsten were the test materials. Both matter for fusion. Beryllium accumulated tritium over four times faster than tungsten. The cleaning tests brought a surprise. Ozone alone did no better than dry air. Ultraviolet light proved to be the required ingredient for real decontamination.
arxiv-2512-24456:
Gentian Zavalani speeds up solving PDEs on surfaces meshed with triangles. A fast direct solver framework exists for meshes built from four-sided cells. Each cell there uses tensor-product basis functions. Triangular meshes were locked out of that framework. Many real surfaces come in triangles, though. Zavalani removes the restriction.

Two high-order strategies handle the triangles. A reduced step converts them into four-sided cells for the existing machinery. A second method builds basis functions on triangles directly, using Dubiner's basis. Tests confirm the changes keep the framework's accuracy. Speed and the fast direct-solver structure survive as well. Time-dependent and moving surfaces are also covered. Reaction-diffusion systems demonstrate the method. Surface flow driven by geometry provides a second demonstration.
arxiv-2512-24556:
Muhammad Abdullahi Said and Muhammad Sammani Sani audit language model safety across languages and time frames. Safety tuning is usually tested in English. Whether it transfers to other languages is often assumed, not checked. The authors build HausaSafety, an adversarial dataset grounded in West African threat scenarios. Three leading models face it in English and Hausa.

A factorial design crosses language with temporal framing across many evaluations. The expected simple story did not appear. One model was safer in Hausa than in English, thanks to uncertainty-driven refusals. A deeper pattern dominated instead. Past-tense framing slipped past defenses badly. Future-tense framing triggered heavy over-refusal. Safety swung widely between the safest and weakest configurations. The authors conclude that models lean on surface heuristics. They propose invariant alignment for safety that survives language and tense shifts.
arxiv-2512-24856:
Sergio Alvarez-Telena and Marta Diez-Fernandez seek conceptual clarity for agentic AI through the lens of algorithmization, their field concerned with turning tasks into algorithms.
