About 1666 he took the rabbinate of Leghorn, a post Jacob Sasportas had declined on Naar's own advice. De Barrios prized him and credits him with a work called Reglas del Din. Whether he is the later medical writer of the same name, the entry leaves open.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neubauer-adolf-:
Adolf Neubauer was Oxford's great keeper of Hebrew manuscripts. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bittse, Hungary, on March 11, 1831. His schooling in rabbinic books was thorough and deep. His first writings appeared in Jewish and French journals.

A mission to St. Petersburg in 1864 changed his path. He examined its many Karaite manuscripts there. His Talmud geography of 1868 made his name. Oxford then hired him to catalogue the Bodleian's Hebrew books. The catalogue came in 1886, after eighteen years. It holds over 2,500 entries and forty facsimiles. He edited Tobit, medieval chronicles, and Isaiah studies. Failing eyes ended his Oxford readership in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissen-nissen-s:
Henriette Nissen was a Swedish singer of great range. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in Göteborg on March 12, 1819. She died in Harzburg on Aug. 27, 1879. She studied piano under Chopin in 1839.

She learned singing under Manuel Garcia at Paris. Her debut came in 1843 as Adalgisa, beside Grisi's Norma. Donizetti himself taught her the role of Irene. Tours of Italy, Russia, and England followed in triumph. At Berlin her fame rivaled Jenny Lind's own. In 1850 she married the violinist Siegfried Saloman. From 1859 she taught singing at St. Petersburg's conservatory. Her book on the study of song appeared in 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ochs-george-was:
George Washington Ochs was an American newsman from Cincinnati. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on October 20, 1861. He was a brother of Adolph Simon Ochs. He was schooled at the University of Tennessee. He began work as a reporter in Chattanooga.

Ochs rose to run the Chattanooga Daily Times by 1896. In 1900 he ran a daily Paris edition for the New York Times. That work won him praise in France. The French head of state gave him a high honor. He then ran papers in Philadelphia with his brother. At home he served two terms as mayor of Chattanooga. He also led the town library board for six years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ordination-1175:
Ordination is the rite that sets a man in high office. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The office is that of judge and teacher of the Law. The rite is a solemn, public act of choice. The custom is a very old one in Israel.

Joshua was set in office by Moses in this way. Moses set him before the priest and the flock. He laid his hands on Joshua and gave him charge. Part of Moses' own spirit passed through those hands. Moses set the seventy elders in office as well. They helped him rule the folk in the wild. By tale, those elders set their heirs in office next. So an unbroken chain of such men ran on through time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palace-11856:
The palace was the great house of a king in Bible lands. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrews learned great building from the Phoenicians. David's palace was built by men sent by Hiram of Tyre. Solomon used those skilled men for his works too.

No facts are known of David's palace, save its site. It stood in the City of David, on Zion's south slope. To the north of it, Solomon built his own palace. It was a vast work that held more than a house. It held the Temple and other great halls in its walls. Its main gate was set on the south side. The first hall named is the House of the Forest. That hall took its name from its cedar posts in rows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pavia-the-ancie:
Pavia is an Italian city on the River Ticino. Jews lived there as early as the eighth century. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city's Jews worked in banking, trade, and farming.

Under the dukes of Milan their lot stayed fairly mild. One threat came from Bernardinus of Feltre, a fiery preacher. The duke barred him from preaching in 1480. Spanish rule brought harder times, with riots and royal decrees. A banishment order of 1566 was never carried out. The yellow cap was forced on Jews that same year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesante-pizante:
Moses ben Hayyim Pesante was a Turkish commentator. He worked in the second half of the sixteenth century. The Executive Committee and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Three works of his reached print. His world was the Ottoman Jewish east.

His Yesha Elohim explains the Hoshanot prayers for Sukkot. It also treats scattered texts and sayings of Scripture. The book came out at Constantinople in 1567. A second edition followed at Salonica two years later. He also glossed Ibn Gabirol's Azharot poem. A third work comments on the Passover Haggadah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polonnoye-12256:
Polonnoye is a town in the district of Novograd in Volhynia, Russia. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town was walled and strong in the mid seventeenth century. At the Cossack rising some 12,000 Jews found shelter inside it.

Two rabbis of the town were Solomon Harif and his son Moses. Moses later became rabbi of Lemberg. Best known was Jacob Joseph ha-Kohen, who died in 1769. His book first set out the teaching of the Baal Shem in print. Angry foes burned the book in the yard at Wilna. The town also kept a Hebrew printing office. Its first known book came out in 1791.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-price-julius-me:
Julius Mendes Price was an English traveler, artist, and journalist. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in about 1858. He studied at University College in London. He studied at Brussels and at an art school in Paris as well.

In 1884 Price went as a war reporter to Bechuanaland. He drew and wrote for the Illustrated London News. He then joined a party bound for inner Siberia. Alone, he crossed Siberia and Mongolia to reach Peking. That hard trip ran through the years 1890 and 1891. He later went with the Greek army in its war with Turkey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quail-12456:
Quail is a bird named in the tale of Israel in the desert. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Exodus and Numbers tell of quails sent as food. The starving people ate them in the wilderness waste. Psalms recall the same gift in later song. It stands as a sign of God's care in want.

Quails still cross the Sinai waste in vast flocks each year. They fly north in spring and south in autumn. They fly very low and soon grow tired. So they fall an easy prey to hunters there. The Talmud counts four kinds of quail in all. The article names those kinds and their marks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rami-b-tamre-12:
Rami b. Tamre was a Babylonian amora of the third generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He came from Pumbedita and likely studied under R. Judah. One visit to Sura made his name known.

The article tells how he arrived on the eve of the Day of Atonement. His conduct there drew notice and a hearing before R. Hisda. He defended himself with a saying of R. Judah. That answer proved him a sharp scholar, the writers say. The entry also sorts out his link to Rami b. Dikuli. Two Talmud passages seem to point in different ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reicher-emanuel:
Emanuel Reicher was an Austrian actor born on July 18, 1849. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Bochnia in Austria. His stage life fell into two clear periods.

The article says his first marriage brought deep unhappiness. That home life held back his acting for years. After his first wife died, he married Lina Harf. She revived the ambition of the discouraged actor. His first success came in Sardou's Theodora at Berlin. He then played Iago opposite Rossi's Othello and triumphed. Modern drama became his true field, they say. He was famed above all for playing Ibsen's characters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-right-of-eminen:
Eminent domain is the state's power to take private land. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Such takings serve public use, especially highways. Pay may or may not be given.

The article quotes the Mishnah on a king's powers. A king may cut a highway for himself without hindrance. Maimonides adds that the road goes straight ahead. It does not bend around one man's field or vineyard. Widths for highways ran from eight to thirty two cubits. The Talmud implies land could be condemned for those roads. It gives no clear procedure for such takings. Later authorities did not discuss the question at all. The entry finds a narrow power, mainly for roads.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenmuller-ern:
Ernst Friedrich Karl Rosenmüller was a Christian Orientalist and theologian born on December 10, 1768. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He became assistant professor of Arabic at Leipsic in 1796.

Rosenmüller gave much of his life to his Scholia in Vetus Testamentum. Its twenty-four parts, issued from 1788 to 1835, gloss the whole Old Testament. Most Bible study of that book in the nineteenth century rested on it. He also wrote early guides to the Old Testament and its antiquities. A pocket edition of the Hebrew Bible from his hand appeared in 1822.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saadia-ben-nahm:
Saadia ben Nahmani was a liturgical poet of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He may also have been a Bible commentator of note.

His hymn for the first evening of Tabernacles opens Sukkat shalem selah. It runs to ten strophes of six lines each in form. Zunz credits him with a second hymn for Sabbaths falling on a month's first day. Scholars link him to the Saadia who spoke with Rashi in person. The Chronicles commentary ascribed to Rashi was arranged by a Saadia's pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samara-13056:
Samara is a Babylonian river near which tradition sets the tomb of Ezra. Joseph Jacobs and J. S. Raisin wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Many legends cluster around that sacred spot on its banks.

Jews and Mohammedans once made pilgrimages there for prayer and relics. A synagogue stood on one side of the tomb, a mosque on the other. Ishmaelites built both, from love of Ezra, yet Jews kept the keys. Al-Harizi tells how a shepherd's dream led diggers to an iron coffin. Its inscription, read by a Jew, named Ezra the priest's grave.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuelson-sir-b:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sir Bernhard Samuelson. He was an English merchant and politician. Samuelson was born at Liverpool on November 22, 1820. He died on May 10, 1905. After an apprenticeship in a Liverpool merchant's office, he ran continental trade for a Manchester engineering firm.

In 1849 Samuelson bought the Agricultural Implement Works at Banbury. In 1854 he built blast furnaces at Middlesborough. He later added collieries and ironstone mines. He sat in Parliament for Banbury from 1865 to 1885. He then represented North Oxfordshire until 1895. In 1881 he joined the Royal Commission on Technical Education. He became its chairman. The entry notes that he had early cut his ties with Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scheindlinger-s:
Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ben Abraham Scheindlinger, called Saler. He was a Polish rabbi. He died at Lemberg on August 7, 1796. He was probably born at Dobromil. He served first as rabbi in Sale. Later he was preacher and head of the court at Lemberg.

Scheindlinger's book Shem mi-Shemu'el appeared at Lemberg in 1817, after his death. Its first part gives sermons arranged by the weekly portions of the Pentateuch. Its second part holds new readings on Talmudic subjects. He left three sons, among them Nathan Hecht of Yaroslav. The entry rests on Buber's Anshe Shem and on Eleazar ha-Kohen's Ḳin'at Soferim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scribes-hebrew-:
Isidore Singer, M. Seligsohn, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the scribes. Their work began as the prophets' activity ceased. Returned exiles from Babylon needed teachers of the Law. Frankel and Krochmal identify the scribes with the men of the Great Synagogue. Ezra was the first of them, and Simeon the Just the last.

The scribes' main task was teaching the Torah to the masses. They built schools and were told to multiply their pupils. Nehemiah shows their method. They read the Hebrew text aloud, translated it, and gave the sense. They also drew the laws out of each passage as they taught. Later ages used soferim in looser ways. It could mean Talmudists in general. At last it shrank to mean teachers of little children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-severus-lucius-:
Lucius Septimius Severus ruled Rome as emperor from 193 to 211. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His reign began in civil war against Pescennius Niger in the East. Most Palestinians backed Niger, while Jewish loyalties stay unclear.

When Severus won, he stripped Neapolis of its citizen rights. Only after his last rival fell in 197 did he lift the punishment. He later marched through Syria after war with Parthia. Palestine likely became its own province at that time. Sebaste gained the rank of a Roman colony. The entry links an emperor's wars to daily status in the Jewish homeland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemariah-ben-e:
Shemariah ben Elhanan headed the yeshivah of Cairo near the end of the tenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His life story begins with a sea capture, tradition says. An Arab admiral seized four scholars sailing from Bari.

The four were raising funds for Babylon's great school. Captors sold Shemariah at Alexandria, where rich Jews ransomed him. He then moved to Cairo and founded a thriving school. Scholars argue over where the four captives came from. Most say Babylonia, while Weiss alone assigns them to Italy. A fragment of Shemariah's responsum supports the Babylonian view. The entry blends adventure, ransom, and the birth of Egyptian Jewish learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silas-13656:
Silas is the name of two men in Josephus's histories of the Jews. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. One Silas made himself tyrant of Lysias in Lebanon. Pompey subdued him on the march to Palestine in 63 B.C.

The second Silas was a friend of King Agrippa the First. He had shared Agrippa's early years of misery. As king, Agrippa made his old comrade general of his troops. Silas then took liberties and kept recalling past sufferings. Agrippa jailed him, freed him, and jailed him again. At last Silas was murdered, seemingly by the king's order. His successor Helkias carried out the killing, Josephus reports. Loyalty soured into insult fills this brief entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simonsen-joseph:
Joseph Levin Simonsen was a Danish jurist born in Copenhagen on December 26, 1814. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He graduated from the University of Copenhagen in law in 1837. In 1851 he was admitted to the bar of the superior court. His legal opinions were quoted as authoritative.

In 1859 Simonsen became vice-president of the Society of Danish Lawyers. From 1848 until his death he served another role as well. He was legal counselor to the Jewish congregation of Copenhagen. That service lasted nearly forty years. He died in his home city on June 21, 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-the-egy: Solomon the Egyptian was physician to the Byzantine emperor Emanuel Comnenus. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He lived at Constantinople in the late twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela visited that city in 1176. He reports that the emperor held Solomon in high esteem. Through Solomon's influence, the Jews of Constantinople gained many advantages. They did so even while living under oppression at the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stocker-adolf-1:
Adolf Stöcker was a German Protestant theologian and anti-Semitic agitator born in 1835. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Halberstadt on December 11. He studied at Halle and Berlin. In 1874 he became court preacher at Berlin's cathedral.

In 1878 Stöcker founded the Christian Socialistic party. From pulpits and public meetings he attacked Jews as a danger. His preaching fed a wider anti-Semitic movement in Germany. Voters sent him to the Prussian Diet in 1879. He also sat in the Reichstag for many years. Berlin dismissed him as court preacher in 1890 over his politics. The entry documents a key figure in modern anti-Semitism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-symmachus-14156:
Symmachus translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek around 200 C.E. Crawford Howell Toy and Felix Perles wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Sources disagree on who he was in faith. Eusebius and Jerome call him an Ebionite Christian. Epiphanius calls him a Samaritan who embraced Judaism.

Symmachus wrote clear Greek, freer of Hebraisms than rivals. He aimed to carry the sense of the original above all. His version won quick and wide recognition. Origen placed it inside his great Hexapla edition. Only fragments of the translation survive today. Field gathered the fullest set of those fragments. Scholars still debate his links to Aquila and Theodotion. The entry weighs a prized version known mainly in pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tartak-14256:
Tartak is a god named just once in the Bible. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Second Kings pairs him with Nibhaz in one verse. Both were gods of the Avites people. Sargon had settled that tribe on Israelite soil.

The Babylonian Talmud says Tartak was worshiped as an ass. Rabbi Judah transmits that claim from Abba Arika. Every try to identify this god has failed so far. No matching deity appears among Babylonians or Assyrians. Egypt offers only a loose parallel for comparison. There the ass was sacred to the god Typhon. Egyptians sacrificed asses to Typhon in his rites. The short entry leaves a one-verse god unsolved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theocracy-greek:
Theocracy means a state where God rules through chosen agents. Kaufmann Kohler and Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Josephus first used the word in this strict sense. He used it for the Jewish government Moses set up under God.

Israel stood as God's own people, a kingdom of priests. Freedom from Egypt made the nation His by right. Moses acted only as God's spokesman to the people. Gideon refused a crown, saying God alone should rule. Wanting a human king counted as rejecting God. Even later kings sat, in effect, on God's throne. Torah law thus flows from the divine King himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tyrnau-or-terna:
Tyrnau, a Hungarian manufacturing town, twice martyred its Jews and banned them forever. Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In 1494 fourteen men and two women died there as martyrs. A Cracow dirge preserves their memory. Turkish invasions later fanned fresh hatred in Hungary.

In 1536 a dead three-year-old boy was found. Citizens accused the Jews of murdering the child. Suspects were executed despite King Ferdinand's peace efforts. In 1539 Ferdinand banished the remaining Jews forever. Leopold confirmed that decree in 1686. A 1717 toll deal briefly let Jews pass through. Maria Theresa annulled even that agreement. Joseph II reopened the city in 1783.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vega-judah-1465:
Judah Vega was a rabbi and preacher in Amsterdam. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Meyer Kayserling wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vega became the first rabbi of Neweh Shalom in 1608. That was Amsterdam's second synagogue. He soon resigned and left for Constantinople in 1610.

At Constantinople, Vega is said to have written a history. It covered Jewish life since the second fall of Jerusalem. He was known as a fine preacher and storyteller. His small book of sermons came out at Lublin in 1616. The entry warns against mixing him up with a namesake. That other Judah Vega taught at Safed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahrmann-judah-: Judah Wahrmann was a Hungarian rabbi, son of Israel Wahrmann. Isidore Singer and Eduard Neumann wrote this brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1791 and died at Pesth on November 14, 1868. In 1851 he became associate rabbi at Budapest. He also taught religion at the city gymnasium. His two books treat copied texts and Mosaic religious teaching. The second of them reached a new edition in 1868.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-well-14856:
A well is a shaft dug down to stored water. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hebrew separates two kinds of wells. A be'er gathers spring or ground water. A bor, or cistern, stores rain water instead.

Jacob's Well, at the foot of Gerizim, survives today. It is twenty three meters deep. Bottle shaped cisterns rank among the oldest forms. Some Temple cisterns were huge in scale. One, called the sea, ran 224 meters around. Covers of stone sealed the drawing hole. That kept people and animals from falling in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wise-stephen-sa:
Stephen Samuel Wise was an American rabbi and the son of Aaron Wise. Cyrus Adler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Budapest, he studied at Columbia and took a doctorate there in 1901. He also trained for the rabbinate with noted teachers in New York.

In 1893 he joined Congregation B'nai Jeshurun in New York as its minister. In 1900 he moved west to lead Congregation Beth Israel in Portland, Oregon. Wise was the first honorary secretary of the American Federation of Zionists. He spoke for English speakers at the Second Zionist Congress in 1898. In Oregon he also worked on child labor rules and public charity boards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yakkar-ben-samu:
Yakkar ben Samuel ha-Levi the Second was a German scholar and hymn poet. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the last half of the 1200s. He worked at Cologne and at Mayence in those years.

He was kin to Meir of Rothenburg, a famed rabbi. Meir names him more than once in his court replies. He had trained with Rabbi Jehiel of Paris as a youth. His side notes on one tract still live in draft form. His hymns fill the rest of the short entry here. One hymn marks the slain of Pforzheim in 1267. Yakkar and his father died in a slaughter in 1271. So that hymn was penned just before his own death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamenhof-lazaru:
Lazarus Ludwig Zamenhof (born 1859) was the founder of the world tongue Esperanto. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Byelostok, he came from a line of tongue teachers. His sire and grandsire both taught French and German tongues.

In 1873 his sire moved the home to Warsaw in Poland. There the sire taught German at two schools in turn. He was one of three Jews to hold such a post then. He rose to the rank of state councilor in time. The son read medicine at Warsaw and at Moscow. He took his degree in the year 1884 there. He set up as an eye doctor at Warsaw in time. His fame rests on the new tongue he made for all men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ziegler-ignaz-1:
Ignaz Ziegler was an Austrian rabbi who held the pulpit at Carlsbad for many years. Isidore Singer and Henry Malter wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Ziegler was born at Also-Kubin, Hungary, on September 29, 1861. He studied at the Rabbinical Seminary and the University of Budapest, taking his doctorate in 1888.

Soon after he graduated, Carlsbad called him as rabbi, and he still held that post in 1905. Through his efforts, a large hospice opened there on May 1, 1903. It gave food, shelter, and medical care to poor Jews who came seeking health. His books include a Hungarian study of the prophet Malachi. Others treat medieval religious debates, Jewish history, and the king parables in the Midrash.
keller-seldwyla-folks-1856:
Wolf von Schierbrand translated three tales from Gottfried Keller's Seldwyla cycle into English in 1919. Seldwyla is Keller's invented Swiss town, full of cheerful idlers and small dreamers. The best-known tale here is A Village Romeo and Juliet, drawn from a real event Keller read in a newspaper.

Two farmers ruin each other over a strip of land between their fields. Their children, Sali and Vrenchen, love in spite of the feud and get one perfect day together. The end is as sad as the day is bright. The other tales mix comedy with the same clear-eyed pity. Keller's Seldwyla stories remain the heart of Swiss prose fiction.
king-henry-vi-part-3-pg2256: York dies on the molehill in this edition: Margaret crowns him with paper before the stabbing, and the wars grind toward Towton. Father kills son, son kills father, in England's bleakest chronicle. The trilogy's blood-soaked climax.
las-casas-tears-of-the-indians-1656:
Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish friar, wrote his Brevísima relación in 1552 to accuse his own nation. The Tears of the Indians is the English translation printed in 1656. Las Casas had lived in the Indies and seen the conquest's cruelty at close range, and he wrote to lay it before the Spanish crown.

His short work lists, region by region, the killings and abuses that followed the Spanish landings. It became the founding text of the Black Legend, the dark fame of Spain's empire abroad. As the first broad indictment of conquest atrocities, it reshaped how Europe argued about empire itself. Its charges still start debate today.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
May 1876 brings Lippincott's minor exhibition structures into view. The century series reaches its fifth paper on the Centennial. Sheila Hale begins two papers of glimpses of Constantinople. Margaret J. Preston contributes The Ballad of the Bell-Tower.

Mrs. Linton advances Leam Dundas through chapters thirty-three to thirty-six. Sidney Lanier offers Rose-Morals for poetry readers. Ivan Tourgueneff's story The Watch appears in translation. Emma Lazarus translates two poems by Heine for the close. An old house and its story join the contents that month. The life of George Ticknor, by Perry, closes the list.
motley-dutch-republic-1856:
John Lothrop Motley published The Rise of the Dutch Republic in 1856, a history of the Netherlands' revolt against Spain. Motley, an American, worked in archives across Europe. William the Silent, Prince of Orange, stands as the hero of the story. Sieges, massacres, and sea battles mark the Dutch fight for freedom.

Motley frames the revolt as a contest between liberty and tyranny. Philip II of Spain plays the villain in his vivid telling. The book won fame in America and Europe alike. Dutch readers embraced it as a national epic in English. It remains the American classic of Dutch history, dramatic and deeply researched for its time.
mr-culpepper-s-treatise-of-aurum-potabil: Mr. Culpepper's Treatise of Aurum Potabile appeared in 1656, on the subject of drinkable gold. Aurum potabile was a famed cordial medicine of the age, gold dissolved for drinking. Surviving fragments of the title page promise a description of the threefold world: elementary, celestial, and intellectual. The hosted sample, however, is mostly garbled OCR from a rough scan. Only fragments of that title page can be read with confidence. Readers therefore get the treatise's identity, date, and subject, but the sample offers no readable argument or recipe.
openalex-w1989554956:
Emanuele Ferri and co-authors checked two ways to name worms. Their study is dated 2009 in the catalog record. The worms are thin parasites of people and beasts. Fast, sure naming is the base for sound work on them. Two routes to a name were put to the test.

One route reads body form and shape under a scope. The other reads a short stretch of DNA as a code. The team scored how well each route told species apart. Each route has its own strengths in speed and trust. Used together, they give the surest names of all. Labs that name these worms gain a clear guide.
openalex-w2159170056:
Bryan Wallace, Andrew DiMatteo, Brendan Hurley, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2010. They propose Regional Management Units, a new framework for setting marine turtle conservation and research priorities. Widely spread sea animals face threats that strike different population segments at different scales, so species-wide labels mislead managers.

The framework defines population segments by combining several tools. Site monitoring, genetics, mark-recapture work, and satellite tracking each reveal structure at its own scale. Merged, they draw robust units that match how threats actually operate. Conservation and research can then be aimed unit by unit. The scale can run from local to global, instead of treating each species as one block.
openalex-w2168545956:
Dan Charman, David Beilman, Maarten Blaauw, and colleagues published this study in Biogeosciences in 2013. They used a large new database of northern peat profiles to track carbon storage over the last thousand years. Peatlands hold vast carbon, and many assumed warming would rot peat faster and release it, feeding further warming.

The records point the other way. Total carbon stored tracked the length of the growing season and available light, not decay rates. Plant growth, it seems, governs long-term storage more than breakdown does. Storage slowed when climate cooled from the medieval warm period into the Little Ice Age. The authors suggest sequestration could rise across many northern peatlands in a warmer future.
openalex-w2184278756:
V. Khachatryan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this study in the European Physical Journal C in 2016. They produced fresh parameter sets, called tunes, for the computer programs that simulate proton collisions. The tunes govern the underlying event, the soft spray of particles around the main clash, and cases where several parton pairs collide at once.

Fits combined CMS data at one energy with older CDF proton-antiproton data at lower energies. Three major generator programs were tuned under several proton structure maps. The authors checked whether the fitted values also matched data sensitive to double-parton scattering. The tunes were tested on many event types and used to predict behavior at the collider's higher energy.
openalex-w2560801056:
The ALICE Collaboration published this measurement in Physical Review Letters in 2016, with J. Adam as first author. It reports how many charged particles appear at midrapidity when lead nuclei collide. The collisions reached 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair, then the highest energy achieved in a laboratory. The team sorted collisions by centrality, meaning how head-on the nuclei struck.

More central collisions involve more participating nucleons and produce more particles. Earlier measurements at lower energies showed particle density rising faster with energy in nucleus collisions than in proton ones. This paper extends that record to the new energy frontier. Its results constrain models of how particles are produced in these crashes. Comparing across energies also tests whether the production mechanism stays the same.
openalex-w2637985556:
Margarita Mulero-Pázmány, Susanne Jenni-Eiermann, and Nicolas Strebel, with colleagues, reviewed how wildlife reacts to drones in this 2017 PLOS ONE paper. Small unmanned aircraft are booming for work and leisure. They fly low over any terrain, bringing them close to animals. Nobody had systematically judged this new kind of human disturbance.

The authors reviewed the existing studies and pooled their data. Reactions depended on the drone's flight pattern, engine type, and size. They also depended on the animal's species, life stage, and group size. Flights aimed straight at animals, larger craft, and noisy fuel engines provoked the strongest responses. Birds reacted more readily than other animal groups. The paper offers guidelines for users, conservationists, and makers, and urges updated laws. Its message: drones are useful tools, but wildlife needs protection from careless flying.
openalex-w2767362256:
Ann Marie Weideman, Marco Aurelio Tapia-Maltos, and Kory R. Johnson, with colleagues, analyzed how age affects multiple sclerosis drugs in Frontiers in Neurology in 2017. Modern disease-modifying therapies tame the immune attacks that drive MS. Whether they keep working as patients age was an open question. The authors suspected efficacy fades as the disease evolves from inflammation toward degeneration.

They meta-analyzed all blinded, randomized trials of immunomodulatory MS drugs that reported disability outcomes. The goal was to test whether drug efficacy is independent of patient age. Their hypothesis: benefit shrinks as age and disease duration grow. They also built age-adjusted models to compare drugs fairly across trials with different patient ages. Such models could help doctors predict what a given patient stands to gain. They also help researchers correct trial results for the therapies patients received.
openalex-w2802205356:
Vanina Guernier, Cyrille Goarant, and Jackie Benschop, with Colleen L. Lau, reviewed leptospirosis in the Pacific Islands in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2018. The metadata record leaves title and authors blank; the sample itself supplies them. Pacific conditions favor this water-borne bacterial disease, and Oceania reports the world's highest incidence. Yet its local patterns in isolated islands were poorly documented.

The team systematically searched four databases plus grey literature, covering 1947 to mid-2017. Their scope spanned twenty-five Pacific islands across Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia, plus Easter Island and Hawaii. Human and animal infections were both included. The review's title reports its theme: the islands harbor diverse pathogens and animal reservoirs. Mapping that diversity is a first step toward control. Neglected diseases stay neglected partly through missing maps like this one.
openalex-w2964483356:
Leonardo Guzmán-Martínez, Ricardo Maccioni, Víctor Andrade, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Pharmacology. It argues that brain inflammation, or neuroinflammation, is a shared feature of neurodegenerative disorders. Such diseases include Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's disease.

In each disease, a key protein unfolds, forms sheet-like structures, and clumps inside neurons, and the clumps are toxic. The authors propose that these protein changes trigger inflammation cascades in the brain. Support cells called glia switch on, release inflammatory signals, and harm neurons further. Toxicity then spreads across brain areas. Framing inflammation as a common thread may point to treatments that work across several diseases at once.
openalex-w3043179056:
Amélio Godoy-Matos, Wellington Silva Júnior, and Cynthia Valério wrote this review in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome in 2020. It presents non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD, as one continuum running from obesity through metabolic syndrome to diabetes. The condition is now the most frequent liver disease in the world.

About a quarter of the global population is affected, often alongside diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. The authors explain the onset as a complex process tied to insulin resistance and struggling fat tissue. A fatty liver also drives hormone changes that feed diabetes itself. They review scan-free tests and scores for fat and scarring, propose a stepwise workup, and discuss treatments borrowed from obesity and diabetes care.
openalex-w3046229056:
Eirini Karyotaki, Pim Cuijpers, Yesica Albor, and colleagues published this study in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It reports data from the World Health Organization's World Mental Health Surveys International College Student Initiative. The subject is the sources of stress in college life and their links to mental disorders.

First-year students in nine countries described the stresses they faced across many life areas. College is a sharp transition, and heavy stress threatens both wellbeing and study success. No large cross-national study had yet ranked these stresses or weighed their share in student disorders. By measuring prevalence and severity together, the team shows which pressures matter most. Such ranking helps universities aim support where it counts.
openalex-w3205344656:
Livio Pagano, Jon Salmanton-García, Francesco Marchesi, and colleagues surveyed COVID-19 in adults with blood cancers across Europe. Their survey, run for the European Hematology Association, appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology in 2021. People with these cancers face high risk from the virus. The team wanted to learn which patients fared worst, and why.

The study gathered more than three thousand eight hundred cases seen between March and December 2020. Nearly two thirds of patients had severe or critical illness, and about three in ten died. Deaths were highest in acute myeloid leukaemia and related disorders. Mortality fell between the first and second pandemic waves, a hopeful sign for care.
openalex-w4296293256:
Victoria Miller, Patrick Webb, Frederick Cudhea, and colleagues measured diet quality in one hundred eighty-five countries, in Nature Food in 2022. Good data on what the world eats are scarce, especially for children. The team drew on the Global Dietary Database, covering 1990 to 2018. They scored diets with the Alternative Healthy Eating Index, a validated scale from zero, least healthy, to one hundred, most healthy.

In 2018 the world average score sat near forty, which the authors call generally modest. Regional averages ran from about thirty in Latin America and the Caribbean to about forty-six in South Asia. Children's scores mostly matched adults' within each region. The gaps by nation, age, education, and city living show where food policy could gain most.
openalex-w4387452756:
Mohammad Chehelgerdi, Matin Chehelgerdi, Omer Allela, and colleagues review nanotechnology for targeted cancer treatment, in Molecular Cancer in 2023. Tiny engineered carriers can ferry drugs straight to tumour cells. Protein engineering and materials science have produced many such nanoscale targeting schemes. A few carriers have won approval for human use, but most stall between the lab bench and the clinic.

The review examines the authorised products and the carriers still in trials. It explains why translation is hard: tumours differ, the body clears particles, and results in animals often fail in people. Safety and manufacturing add further hurdles. The authors argue the platform still promises better detection and treatment, if the bottlenecks get solved.
openalex-w7204275056:
Helane Cristina de Andrade Rodrigues Severo led a Portuguese-language greenhouse experiment, in Brazil in 2026. On inoculating a eucalyptus clone with beneficial root fungi and feeding it with bokashi, a fermented organic fertilizer. The trial at the Federal University of Piauí crossed six fungal treatments, using three fungus species alone and joined, plus an uninoculated control, with five doses of a commercial bokashi product. Ninety days after planting, the team measured seedling growth.

Fungal treatment and fertilizer dose interacted greatly for plant height, root dry mass, root length, and fungal colonization. One fungus colonized roots strongly even when nutrients were scarce, and combinations boosted root growth. Overall, the clone's response depended jointly on nutrient availability and symbiotic efficiency, a result growers can use when raising forest seedlings.
openalex-w7204586256:
João Victor de Sousa Coutinho led a Portuguese-language laboratory study, in Brazil in 2026, comparing the smoke point of oil extracted from the bullfrog with extra virgin olive oil and soybean oil. The smoke point measures a fat's heat resistance; cooking oils need stability so they do not degrade and release toxic substances. The team extracted frog oil with a solvent, characterized it by gas chromatography, and heated all three oils on a hot plate while watching for smoke.

Frog oil proved rich in polyunsaturated fats, including omega 3, 6, and 9 families. Its smoke point was the highest of the three, above both olive and soybean oil. The authors conclude that bullfrog oil has real potential for gastronomic use in food preparations.
openalex-w7205008356:
Alessandra Maranhão Bordadagua Nunes led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on ultrasound-guided puncture by nurses inserting PICC lines, peripherally inserted central catheters. Ultrasound lets nurses see vascular structures in real time, raising precision, cutting problems, and improving safety, above all for patients with difficult venous access such as newborns, children, and the critically ill. The review searched a health library's sources for 2020 to 2025 full papers and selected sixteen publications.

Ultrasound guidance greatly raised first-attempt success, the studies showed, reduced repeated attempts, and lowered problems such as hematomas, infiltrations, phlebitis, and early catheter loss. Benefits also reached patient safety and care quality. The review maps where the technique stands for nursing practice and what problems remain in training and adoption.
openalex-w7206176456:
Apoliana Carola Rodrigues and five colleagues report a school project called Prato Consciente, or Conscious Plate, at an early-childhood school in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceara, Brazil. Food waste is a social, economic, and teaching problem, and school lunchrooms are no exception. The 2026 project set out to build sustainable eating habits, cut the food children throw away, and bring composting into daily school life.

Activities mixed fun talks, booklets, picture materials, and a wall panel nicknamed the waste meter that showed children how much was discarded. In a workshop, nearly all the children built mini composters from plastic bottles. Project records estimate that leftover food fell by about a third afterward. The authors note limits: no regular weighing, a short follow-up, and one school only, so wider claims need care.
openalex-w7212443156:
Dinomar Alves Moreira and Halline Cardoso Jurema review nursing care in childbirth of the kind called humane. In that kind, the woman leads: her voice, her pose, and her wish to have kin at her side. The pair read past work from 2013 to 2019 in two Latin health stores. Six studies made the cut. They asked what part the nurse plays when birth is run this way.

The nurse, the work shows, is the core of the humane turn. Nurses guard the woman's free will and cut needless steps. They teach, stay close, and keep her calm. The gains show in fast heal time, a strong first bond with the child, and fewer harms. Bars stand in the way: thin training and poor space in health posts. The review thus backs the obstetric nurse as the one who makes birth both safe and kind.
openalex-w7213966156:
Vinícius Leon Lyra de Menezes and colleagues study teachers and youth mental health in Cáceres, Mato Grosso. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covers major depression and anxiety disorders among public school pupils. Secondary education data for 2025 were analysed, and ninety pedagogy and language students answered structured questionnaires.

Among more than eight thousand enrolled pupils, only nine held a formal recorded diagnosis, suggesting strong under-recording. Future teachers knew the disorders only in part and felt unsure handling pupils in psychic distress. School is a key place to spot early signs, the authors argue, and teachers are front-line observers. Wider teacher training and stronger school support are needed to close that recognition gap.
openalex-w7214901456:
Juliana Kemelly da Silva Bezerra, Thauani Achilly Aparecida Teixeira, and Micheli Patrícia de Fátima Magri reviewed, in 2026, the nurse's role in preventing and caring for breast cancer in women. Their narrative review, guided by standard reporting steps, screened the literature from 2020 to 2026 and kept forty-six studies. Breast and cervical cancers weigh heavily on women's health and well-being worldwide, and nurses meet patients across the whole path.

Primary care and health education emerged as pillars for early diagnosis and for overcoming barriers to screening, such as fear and embarrassment. Organized nursing care processes structure technical and humanized care. Diagnosis shakes self-image, self-esteem, and sexuality, so family and social support, active listening, and a trusting bond matter. The authors conclude nursing plays a strategic role in lowering deaths and improving quality of life by joining prevention with whole-person care.
openalex-w7214912356:
Lucas Rêto Batista led a 2026 review of eye damage in congenital toxoplasmosis, an infection passed to a baby before birth by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. Searching four databases for observational studies and controlled trials from the past decade, the team selected twenty-five articles. The infection can severely affect newborns' eyes, and the review maps which signs appear most and why.

Inflammation of the retina and the layer beneath it was by far the most common form, reported in nearly all studies. Retinal bleeding, cataract, inflammation inside the eye, and retinal detachment also appeared. The damage comes from an intense inflammatory response in the fetus's still-growing eye tissues, for which the parasite shows a strong pull. The authors conclude congenital toxoplasmosis remains a relevant cause of childhood vision loss, with that retinal inflammation as its leading form.
openalex-w7221065256:
Maickelly Cristina Dourado Batista and Esley Porto examined whether Brazilian courts can order compensation when parents emotionally abandon their children, in a 2026 family law study. The question turns on a fine distinction: parents owe legal duties of care, presence, and upbringing, even though no law can command them to feel affection.

Reading statutes, doctrine, and court decisions, they find civil liability possible when unlawful conduct, harm, and a causal link are proven, covering moral and sometimes material damages. A 2025 law strengthened the ground by naming affective abandonment an unlawful act in the child and adolescent statute. Each case, they stress, must be judged on its own facts, with the child's dignity first.
openalex-w7221125856:
Silvelene Carneiro de Sousa and Antônio Carlos Freire Sampaio studied the sharps safety committee of the Hospital de Clínicas de Uberlândia, in a 2026 article. Needles and blades injure health workers often, and Brazilian regulation requires hospitals to run multidisciplinary committees that prevent and manage such accidents.

Interviewing seven committee representatives, half the group's membership, the authors describe a body charged with cutting accidents at their source. National safety rule number thirty-two anchors the committee's authority and workers' rights. The study presents this committee work as slow construction: it protects staff only when the whole institution and its professionals back it. Their account shows occupational safety as an organizational habit, not a poster.
owen-mortification-of-sin-1656:
John Owen was the leading Puritan theologian of Cromwell's England, dean and vice-chancellor at Oxford. His Mortification of Sin in Believers, published in 1656, is a searching treatise on killing indwelling sin. Owen wrote it first for students, then for all serious believers.

He argues that sin, left alone, never fades but grows, so the believer must make its death a daily business. The work is God's Spirit's, Owen insists, yet it demands watchfulness, prayer, and honest self-knowledge from us. Puritan and evangelical readers still treat the treatise as the sharpest probe of the inner life.
paracelsus-supreme-mysteries-nature-1656:
Paracelsus reached English readers in force with the 1656 Turner collection, Of the Supreme Mysteries of Nature. The Swiss physician and alchemist had been dead a century, yet his fame kept growing. Spirits of the planets, the magical cure of wounds, and the secrets of the twelve zodiac signs fill these treatises.

Paracelsus taught that nature hides powers the bold physician can learn to use. Occult philosophy and hands-on cure mix freely in his pages, as they did in his practice. The volume stands as the key early-modern English Paracelsus, a door into Renaissance medicine and magic alike.
paracelsvs-of-the-supreme-mysteries-of-n: Paracelsus of the Supreme Mysteries of Nature is dated 1656 in the catalog. Robert Turner translated the work into English. Its full title promises the spirits of the planets and occult philosophy. The magical cure of wounds and diseases follows. The mysteries of the twelve signs of the zodiac close it. The hosted sample shows the digitization notice and a garbled title opening only. The scan's letters are too broken to read further. This note therefore rests on the catalog title alone, and claims nothing of the text.
picatrix-castilian-alfonso-1256:
Astral magic fills the Picatrix, in the Castilian version made in 1256 for Alfonso the Wise of Castile. Talismans, planetary spirits, and the powers of the stars crowd its pages. The Arabic compendium, ascribed to al-Majriti, passed through the learned king's scriptorium into the most famous grimoire of the Middle Ages in any tongue.

Images are carved, fumigations burned, and hours chosen by the stars. Court scholars rendered the work as Buqratis in their Romance vernacular. Its lore shaped ritual magic in Europe for centuries afterward in secret. Readers meet medieval learned magic at its fullest, in the very dress that Alfonso's translators gave it at his command.
plos-pbio-0020356:
Daniel Hostetter, Sarah Rice, Sara Dean, and their team studied a slime mold motor protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Myosin is the motor that pulls on actin in muscle and in many other cells. In the slime mold Dictyostelium, myosin strands bundle into thick filaments with two ends pointing outward.

The authors tested which parts of the protein, and which electric charges on it, drive that bundling. Getting the bundles right is vital for the cell to divide and crawl. Slime molds are a favored test bed for such motors. The fine rules found here help explain how myosin assembles in all cells, including the muscle cells whose failure causes some human myopathies.
plos-pone-0000056:
Paul Vigne and Christian Frelin reported a dietary surprise from fruit fly research in 2006. Drosophila, the fruit fly, is a stand-in for studying how bodies handle stress. Hypoxic tolerance is the ability to survive low oxygen, which matters in strokes, heart attacks, and high altitude. Diet is an unlikely lever for it.

Flies raised on a low protein diet showed increased tolerance to low oxygen. A simple change in food shifted a hard physiological limit. Findings like this do not transfer straight to people. But they reveal that oxygen survival is tunable by metabolism. They also give researchers a cheap model in which to find the tuning knobs.
plos-pone-0000156:
Hong J. Lee, Kwang S. Kim, In H. Park, and colleagues published this stroke study in PLOS ONE in 2007. The team used human neural stem cells engineered to over-produce VEGF, a factor that grows blood vessels. The cells were tested in a mouse model of stroke, where a blocked vessel starves part of the brain.

The title sums up the outcome: the treated mice gained protection for neurons, new vessel growth, and better functional recovery. Stem cells plus VEGF is a two-pronged approach, replacing support while rebuilding supply lines. The results encouraged work on cell therapy for stroke, where human treatments remain scarce.
plos-pone-0000256:
Michael J. Morgan, William McEwan, and Joshua Solomon published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a person stares at the center of a textured patch, holes in the texture's edge rapidly fade from view, creating an artificial blind spot. The authors study the lingering effects of that artificial scotoma after the staring ends.

Vision fills in missing patches so smoothly that the brain hides its own gaps. This study measures what the filling-in leaves behind. The findings bear on how the visual system maintains a seamless world from a retina that actually has holes and interruptions in it.
plos-pone-0000356:
Gaëll Mainguy, Jan Koster, Joost Woltering, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hox clusters, the gene rows that pattern animal bodies, were thought to be read one gene at a time in the forward direction. The authors report extensive polycistronism and antisense transcription in the mammalian Hox clusters: long messages spanning several genes, and messages read off the opposite strand.

That messiness revises the tidy picture of Hox regulation. Long multi-gene transcripts and antisense copies add control layers to a famous system. The findings matter for developmental biology, where the precision of Hox activity builds the body plan.
plos-pone-0000456:
Y.-H. Percival Zhang and colleagues built an artificial enzyme pathway that makes hydrogen fuel from starch, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrogen is a clean fuel, but making it without fossil energy is hard. Their synthetic enzymatic pathway uses a designed set of enzymes to convert starch and water into hydrogen at high yield.

Starch is cheap, renewable, and easy to store, unlike hydrogen gas itself. A high-yield route from starch could turn crops or waste biomass into fuel where it is needed. The study is a proof of concept for synthetic biology applied to energy: assembling enzymes from different organisms into a pathway nature never built.
plos-pone-0000556:
Nigel E. Raine and Lars Chittka asked why bumblebees prefer the flower colors they do, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The bee is Bombus terrestris, a common pollinator. The team tested the adaptive significance of sensory bias in a foraging context: whether innate floral colour preferences help bees find food faster.

A sensory bias is a built-in tilt of the senses, and it might be a leftover or a useful shortcut. If naive bees' color preferences match rewarding flowers, the bias speeds learning and earns its keep. Linking a mental quirk to foraging success is how behavioral ecology explains why animal senses are tuned the way they are.
plos-pone-0000656:
Emmanuel J. Chang, Rashida Begum, Brian T. Chait and colleagues worked on predicting where a key cell-cycle enzyme family acts, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cyclin-dependent kinases, or Cdks, add phosphate tags to proteins. That tagging sits at the center of the eukaryotic cell-division cycle. It steers processes such as DNA replication by switching regulators on or off.

Knowing a kinase's substrates, the proteins it tags, is the hard part. Prediction narrows thousands of proteins to likely targets for lab testing. Each confirmed substrate adds a wire to the cell cycle's circuit diagram. The work serves anyone mapping how division is controlled, and how it fails in disease.
plos-pone-0000756:
Jeffrey T.-J. Huang, F. Markus Leweke, Tsz M. Tsang and colleagues profiled spinal fluid from people in the earliest stage before psychosis. The initial prodromal state is an early phase before overt psychosis, marked by sub-threshold or unspecific psychiatric symptoms. Little was known about the biochemical changes during this period, when intervention might help most.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study measured metabolic and proteomic profiles in cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid around brain and spine. Patterns there could flag who is truly heading toward psychosis. Early, objective markers would change psychiatry, which still diagnoses psychosis mainly by symptoms that arrive late in the disease's course.
plos-pone-0000856:
Bruno Marques, Lavinia Liguori, Marie-Hélène Paclet and colleagues delivered a missing enzyme into cells using fat bubbles, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gp91 phox is a transmembrane protein and the catalytic core of the NADPH oxidase complex of neutrophils, the machinery that makes microbe-killing oxidants. Lack of this protein causes chronic granulomatous disease, a rare genetic disorder of severe, recurrent infections, because phagocytes cannot kill what they swallow.

Liposome-mediated delivery carried active gp91 phox into cells. Replacing a membrane protein is far harder than replacing a soluble one, since it must land in the membrane correctly oriented. Success here is a step toward protein-replacement therapy for CGD.
plos-pone-0000956:
Anjon Audhya, Ian McLeod, John Yates and colleagues identified a fourth subunit of a protein sorting machine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. After a receptor is pulled inside the cell, it can keep signaling from internal compartments. To shut it down, the cell buds it into tiny inner vesicles where it is cut off from the cytoplasm.

That sorting is run by the ESCRT machines. The team name a new part, MVB-12, as a fourth subunit of the metazoan ESCRT-I complex, and tie it to receptor downregulation. Each new part clarifies how cells silence signals on time. Failures in that timing are linked to growth disorders and cancer.
plos-pone-0001056:
Eva Sarndahl, Ida Bergstrom, Veronika Brodin and colleagues checked the activation state of neutrophils in stable heart artery disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neutrophils are fast response immune cells, and they have emerged as players in building artery plaques. In unstable angina they are highly activated in the blood.

A primed state had also been proposed for patients with stable angina, a milder claim needing a direct test. The team measured activation status in stable coronary artery disease. Whether quiet looking disease still runs hot immune cells affects how risk is judged. It also bears on whether calming neutrophils could help.
plos-pone-0001156:
Hosts and parasites evolve against each other over generations, often through matching sets of resistance and attack genes. Andy Fenton and Michael Brockhurst modeled a complication in that arms race in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The complication is epistasis, where the effect of one gene depends on another.

Fitness costs of resistance and virulence genes are thought to steer this gene-for-gene coevolution. The authors ask how interactions among several such genes change the dynamics when more than one locus is involved. Their model matters for predicting how resistance, in crops or in medicine, holds up or breaks down over time.
plos-pone-0001256:
Hormone-dependent breast cancers need estrogen to grow, so antiestrogen drugs are a mainstay of treatment, yet resistance is a major cause of failure. Hemant Varma, Andrew Skildum, and Susan Conrad report a route to that resistance in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is pRb, the retinoblastoma protein, a brake on the cell division cycle.

The authors show that functional ablation of pRb activates the cell-cycle enzyme Cdk2 and causes antiestrogen resistance in human breast cancer cells. Losing one brake lets cells keep dividing despite the drug. The mechanism suggests where resistant tumors might be attacked.
plos-pone-0001356:
Why some trauma patients develop wound infections while others do not remains unclear, despite better understanding of trauma itself. Yiorgos Apidianakis and colleagues used a fruit fly infection model to hunt for host genes involved, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A Drosophila melanogaster and Pseudomonas aeruginosa injury and infection model was used to identify host genetic components of susceptibility.

The authors report involvement of the skeletal muscle gene regulatory network in susceptibility to wound infection following trauma. Muscle genes are an unexpected place to find immune vulnerability. The fly model's speed lets such networks be screened in a way human studies cannot.
plos-pone-0001456:
Shannon Williamson and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study from a world ocean sampling voyage. Viruses are the most common life forms on Earth. In the sea they shape gene flow, species mix, and carbon cycles. The team read virus genes from water samples drawn from seas across the globe.

Their reads map which virus types live in each sea zone and how they differ. Most virus genes they found were new to science. That scale of novelty shows how little of the sea virus world is known. The data set gives a base map for ocean health and climate work alike.
plos-pone-0001556:
Aric Gregson and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot built on a hepatitis core shell. The shell bears parts of the malaria parasite's surface protein. The phase 1 trial enrolled 51 healthy adults with no past malaria, aged 18 to 45. Doses rose in steps to test safety first.

The team tracked side effects and immune replies at each dose. A shell that can carry malaria parts on a proven base is a draw for shot design. Clean safety and a firm reply would earn wider trials. Each such step tests the multi part shot idea for malaria.
plos-pone-0001656:
Rudolf S. N. Fehrmann, Hendrik J. M. de Jonge, Arja ter Elst, and their co-authors proposed a new way to read gene activity data in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A gene's output, they note, reflects the joint push of many regulators, which they call transcriptional system regulators. Measuring that joint push across the whole set of genes is hard.

Their approach, called TSR profiling, uses principal component analysis on gene activity data from 17 studies to extract broad regulatory patterns. The full text sets out the method, the data sets, and the profiles it produced. A profile of the whole regulatory system, rather than single genes, could help researchers compare cell states. It could also help them spot disease patterns and check how treatments shift a cell's program.
plos-pone-0001756:
Jay H. Russell and Kenneth C. Keiler screened a bacterium for proteins that sit in set places inside the cell, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Precise protein localization underlies motility, chemotaxis, cell-cycle progression, and cell division in bacteria. How many proteins are localized in any one species was unknown.

Their screen in Caulobacter crescentus used transposon mutagenesis to tag proteins. Caulobacter is famous for its asymmetric division, and the screen revealed which proteins gather at poles or other landmarks. The full text gives the screen design and the localized proteins found. A census of localized proteins shows how much internal geography even a single cell maintains, and gives targets for studying cell polarity.
plos-pone-0001856:
Bin Wang and co-authors studied a protein that steers stem cell fate after spinal injury, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Neural stem and progenitor cells can differentiate into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. They are considered valuable for cell therapy of central nervous system injuries. Transplanted into the adult spinal cord, however, they mostly become astrocytes rather than neurons.

The team reports that Nogo-66 promotes differentiation of neural progenitors into the astroglial lineage through the mTOR-STAT3 pathway. Nogo-66 is a myelin protein known for blocking nerve fiber growth. The full text gives the cell culture results. Knowing what pushes stem cells toward scar-forming astrocytes is a step toward steering them toward repair instead.
plos-pone-0001956:
Shan Yu Fung, Hong Yang, and P. Chen studied tiny self-building peptides as drug carriers, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The cargo was ellipticine, a drug that kills cancer cells but hates water, so it clumps and fails to reach tumors in the body. Certain peptides fold and group on their own and can hold such drugs in a stable mix.

The team varied the peptide sequence and tested how each change shaped the drug complex and its cancer-killing power in lab cells. Sequence is the one dial they can turn freely. Learning which sequences hold the drug best is a step toward carriers that work in patients.
plos-pone-0002056:
Jun Xu and Colleen Clancy modeled burst firing in hippocampal neurons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Some neurons fire in bursts, tight volleys of spikes rather than single ones. In the hippocampus, bursts make signal relay more reliable, yet bursting can also sync networks in the runaway way seen in epilepsy.

The pair built a model of CA3 pyramidal neurons, a main hippocampal cell type, to find the ionic currents that create their inborn bursting. Knowing which currents set the burst points to drugs that could calm sync without silencing normal traffic. Models like this guide the search before lab tests.
plos-pone-0002156:
Jakob Brodersen, Anders Nilsson, Jeppe Ammitzbøll, and co-authors modeled how fish should swim when they migrate against a current, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many fish travel long distances in winter, moving between habitats of unlike quality. Migration burns energy, so the best timing and speed depend on more than where food is best.

The authors worked out the swimming speed that should serve a fish best in a head current. How that choice changes the distance it can cover. Their model gives a benchmark for judging real fish: those that match it are spending their strength wisely on the journey north or south.
plos-pone-0002256:
Irina Harris, Paul Dux, Claire Benito, and co-authors asked at which stage of seeing an object's orientation gets fixed, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A standing debate in vision science concerns the shapes we store for recognition. Do they depend on the angle we saw the object from, or stay the same across angles? The answer may differ by stage of processing.

The team used repetition priming, where seeing an item once speeds its later naming, to probe each stage. Their results show orientation sensitivity varies across the stages of object processing. Work like this helps model how the brain recognizes a chair as a chair from any side.
plos-pone-0002356:
Kholiswa Ngumbela and co-authors measured how weak codon usage slows HIV protein making in T cells. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Wild HIV-1 strains carry genomes low in the letters G and C, with codon choices that human cells read inefficiently. Rewriting a gene with better codons is known to raise protein output in lab vectors.

The team quantified the effect for the viral gag gene inside intact T cells, the very cells HIV infects. Suboptimal codons cut the translational efficiency of the gag message. Knowing the size of that brake matters for vaccine design, where gag protein amounts decide how strong an immune lesson the vaccine teaches.
plos-pone-0002456:
Research by Balleza and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Enrique Balleza, Elena R. Alvarez-Buylla, Alvaro Chaos, and others. Its subject is critical Dynamics in Genetic Regulatory Networks: Examples from Four Kingdoms. The genes of an organism must switch on and off in a coordinated way for the organism to keep working.

That coordination must hold up even when random outside shocks hit the organism. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002556:
Sahin and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Annelise Sahin, Bertrand Daignan-Fornier, Isabelle Sagot, and others. Its subject is polarized Growth in the Absence of F-Actin in Saccharomyces cerevisiae Exiting Quiescence. Polarity establishment and maintenance are crucial for morphogenesis and development.

In budding yeast, these two intricate processes involve the superposition of regulatory loops between polarity landmarks, RHO GTPases, actin-mediated vesicles transport and endocytosis. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002656:
Work by Martin Widschwendter and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was epigenotyping in peripheral blood cell DNA and breast cancer risk: a proof of principle study. The catalog record names Martin Widschwendter first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Epigenetic changes are emerging as one of the most important events in carcinogenesis. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002756:
Work by Eric A. Zilli and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the influence of markov decision process structure on the possible strategic use of working memory and episodic memory. Authorship is credited in the record to Eric A. Zilli and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Researchers use a variety of behavioral tasks to analyze the effect of biological manipulations on memory function. The authors add a further point. This research will benefit from a systematic mathematical method for analyzing memory demands in behavioral tasks. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002856:
Work by Mary-Lee Dequéant and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was comparison of pattern detection methods in microarray time series of the segmentation clock. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Mary-Lee Dequéant, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. While genome-wide gene expression data are generated at an increasing rate, the repertoire of approaches for pattern discovery in these data is still limited. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002956:
Robin Lee, Lawrence Puente, Mads Kærn and co-authors found a non-death job for a yeast metacaspase in 2008. Caspase proteins are best known for carrying out apoptosis, planned cell death. In higher organisms they also shape growth, division, and specialization, beyond killing cells.

In baker's yeast, the metacaspase Yca1p altered cell cycle dynamics, the timing of cell division, the authors report. That is a role apart from death. Published in PLOS ONE, the study broadens how these old proteins are viewed and may inform work on caspases in human disease. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003056: Daniel DiGiulio, Roberto Romero, Harold Amogan and colleagues investigated microbes in amniotic fluid during preterm labor in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The title states the work combined molecular methods with culture-based methods, the two main ways to detect and identify microbes. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, while its abstract snippet repeats the title without further detail. The study reports microbial prevalence, diversity, and abundance in amniotic fluid from preterm labor cases, a topic tied to infection and early birth.
plos-pone-0003156:
Yana V. Bernatavichute, Xiaoyu Zhang, Shawn Cokus and colleagues map two linked marks on DNA in a model plant in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Methylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 is a hallmark of gene silencing in many organisms. In Arabidopsis thaliana, one form of that mark helps silence transposons and control DNA methylation.

The team built a high-resolution genome-wide map to test how this histone mark associates with CHG DNA methylation. Readers see the two silencing systems laid out across the whole genome. The work helps explain how plants keep mobile DNA quiet without harming normal genes.
plos-pone-0003256: Jie Zhong and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on a vaccine against human cytomegalovirus, a common herpesvirus. The title states its aim: to bring about broad protective immunity after vaccination with a chimeric vaccine, one built from mixed parts. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no results.
plos-pone-0003356:
Chihiro Hiramatsu, Amanda D. Melin, Filippo Aureli and colleagues test primate fruit finding in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Trichromatic primates have a red-green chromatic channel in addition to luminance and blue-yellow channels. It has been argued that the red-green channel evolved in primates as an adaptation for detecting reddish or yellowish objects, such as ripe fruits, against a background of foliage.

The authors assess importance of achromatic contrast in short-range fruit foraging of primates. Readers learn brightness contrast may matter more than colour at close range. That nuance revises a classic story about why primates evolved colour vision.
plos-pone-0003456:
Rahul Regulapati and co-authors proposed an origin for split genes in this 2008 paper. Genes of complex cells come in pieces, coding parts split by long non-coding stretches. Why genes took that fractured form stayed unsolved for thirty years. The authors focused on genes of the spliceosome, the machine that joins the pieces.

They argue the split structure could arise from random genetic sequences. Their solution claims to explain the pattern without special design. A random start would make split genes a byproduct of chance. The paper offers a testable story for a basic puzzle of biology.
plos-pone-0003556:
Semir Zeki and John Paul Romaya scanned the brain during hate in this 2008 study. Hate is a strong emotion that science had barely explored with imaging. Seventeen volunteers lay in a scanner for the tests. Each viewed the face of a person they hated.

They also viewed faces of acquaintances who stirred no strong feeling. Comparing the two sets mapped the neural correlates of hate. The active pattern was distinct from neutral face viewing. Mapping base emotions helps explain behavior driven by them. Hate drives real-world violence, which makes its brain roots worth mapping.
plos-pone-0003656:
Yuh-Man Sun, Megan Cooper, Sophie Finch, and colleagues published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. As stem cells become neurons, whole sets of genes must switch off and on in order. REST is a protein that shuts down neuron genes in non-neural cells.

The team found REST also controls genes for the extracellular matrix, the mesh that surrounds and supports cells. That control proved crucial for neural development to proceed well. The study widens REST's role beyond switching genes off inside the cell. It also shapes the scaffold the growing brain builds around itself.
plos-pone-0003756:
Christian Krintel, Peter Osmark, Martin R. Larsen, and colleagues published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hormone-sensitive lipase is a key enzyme that frees fatty acids from stored fat. Its activity is switched on by phosphorylation, the adding of phosphate tags. Protein kinase A does much of that switching.

Working on the human enzyme, the team found two serine sites, 649 and 650, matter most. Those spots are the major determinants of activation by protein kinase A against fat substrates. The precise mapping shows exactly where the body flips its fat-release switch.
plos-pone-0003856:
Eduardo R. Ropelle, Maria Fernanda A. Fernandes, Marcelo B. S. Flores, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. AMPK and mTOR are key regulators of the cell's energy balance and of how leptin, the satiety hormone, curbs food intake. Acute exercise makes animals more sensitive to leptin.

The team asked whether exercise acts in the brain's control centers on those energy sensors. They found exercise increases the AMPK and mTOR response to leptin there. The result shows physical activity rewiring appetite control at the molecular level, not just burning calories.
plos-pone-0003956:
Dennis Eckmeier, Bart R. H. Geurten, Daniel Kress, and co-authors studied how zebra finches use vision in flight in 2008. Fast-flying animals read optic flow, the motion pattern across the eye. Flow from straight flight carries depth cues about the surroundings. Flow from turning carries no such depth information.

Their PLOS ONE article asks how free-flying finches solve that mix. The birds must separate turning from straight motion to judge space. Their gaze strategy likely steadies the image during key moments. The work explains how small birds navigate clutter at speed. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004056:
Christine Stabell Benn, Ane Bærent Fisker, Amabelia Rodrigues, and co-authors studied birth vaccines in Guinea-Bissau in 2008. Oral polio vaccine at birth was policy in many low-income countries. The policy aimed to raise coverage of the vaccine. Its effect on overall infant survival was never studied.

During a vitamin A trial there, some newborns missed the polio vaccine at birth. That accident created a natural experiment on the policy. Their PLOS ONE article reports effects that differed between boys and girls. Such non-target effects matter for vaccine schedules worldwide. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004156:
Karli Watson, Jason Ghodasra, and Michael Platt published this primate study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Serotonin signalling shapes social behaviour in humans and other primates. In humans, a variant near the serotonin transporter gene affects social anxiety and how strongly the amygdala reacts to social cues.

The team asked whether the same gene variant changes how rhesus macaques respond to social reward and punishment. Linking gene variants to social choices in monkeys helps separate biology from upbringing. The study gives a controlled animal window on how one gene can tilt social life.
plos-pone-0004256:
Rachel Lubong Sabado and colleagues published this HIV immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. What it takes to prime HIV-specific T cells, and why those responses look the way they do in infected people, remained undefined. In lymph nodes, T cells must touch dendritic cells to activate, and that same contact can pass HIV between cells.
