Security rules fail when staff see them as someone else's job, so employee perspectives are the real test of a policy. An exploratory study maps attitudes before a company tries to change them. Energy firms guard data whose loss could affect markets and infrastructure, making their staff's habits a matter of wider interest to security managers.
plos-pone-0349756:
Soichiro Takamiya and colleagues asked a pricing question: at what cost would stem cell therapy for stroke be good value in Japan? A recent combined analysis of trials found the therapy helps patients after acute or early stroke, but the treatment will not be cheap. The team built a ten-year simulation comparing stem cells plus standard care against standard care alone.

The model tracked costs and quality-adjusted life years, the standard measure blending length and quality of life. Working backward from Japan's official value threshold, they solved for the therapy price at which the extra benefit justifies the extra cost. Health systems need exactly this number before a promising therapy can be covered, priced, and offered fairly.
plos-pone-0349856:
Sileshi Demelash Sasie and colleagues evaluated the disease surveillance system of Ethiopia's Sidama Region, the network meant to spot outbreaks early. One hundred forty health workers and facilities across thirteen districts were checked against World Health Organization and national standards, covering case detection, reporting, data analysis, training, and supplies. The survey ran in late 2023.

Evaluations like this score each link in the chain, from village health posts to regional offices, against set adherence targets. Weak links, such as late reports or missing feedback, are exactly where an outbreak can slip through unseen. With few subnational evaluations published in Ethiopia, a district-by-district account gives regional managers concrete gaps to fix rather than general worry.
plos-pone-0350556:
Sorachai Kamollimsakul and co-authors followed university students through a self-guided meditation program to see if each short session lifted mood on the spot. Students report high stress, and formal services are often hard to reach. Their 2026 study had twenty-seven students complete twenty-eight sessions of a Thai mind-body practice over two weeks, rating negative mood just before and after each session.

Students stuck with the program well, finishing nearly all sessions. Negative mood dropped clearly right after every session, and that lift stayed steady across the two weeks rather than fading. Starting levels of anxiety and resilience did not change the benefit. The authors present the practice as a feasible per-session mood tool for similar student groups, while calling the evidence preliminary.
plos-pone-0350656:
Tereza Patrmanova and colleagues compared soils under native beech trees and planted spruce trees at one European site. Tree type shapes soil chemistry and microbes, which in turn steer how soil forms and stores carbon. Samples across soil layers were tested for acidity, nutrients, dissolved carbon forms, carbon makeup, and microbe communities.

Total carbon stored did not differ between forests. Carbon quality and its spread across layers did differ. Spruce soil showed acid washing changes absent under beech, and one dissolved acid ran far higher. Beech soil, milder and richer in easy carbon, hosted distinct microbe groups. Swapping tree species changes what soil carbon is, even when totals look the same.
plos-pone-0350856:
Clara L Sanchez and colleagues asked whether heart rhythm wobble can tell what kind of exercise a person is doing. Knowing dose matters when activity itself acts as treatment. Twenty six healthy volunteers cycled at two steady loads and in bursts, while chest straps logged each beat and gas and lactate measures tracked effort.

Beats from the last four minutes of each bout fed a model that sorted sessions by type. Correct sorting was strong, with hit and clear rates in the high eighties to high nineties. Simple beat spread measures and a fractal style index carried most signal. A cheap chest strap, the work hints, may reveal exercise pattern where diaries stay vague.
plos-pone-0350956:
Brooke Ike leads a team of six publishing the plan for a pilot trial of social prescribing against loneliness in cancer survivors, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Social prescribing, a British model, connects patients to community activities and support through a link worker rather than a prescription pad. The team adapted a proven version for survivors using a structured adaptation process, then designed a feasibility trial across two primary care practices serving rural patients in the American Northwest.

Thirty-six survivors who screen positive for loneliness will be assigned by chance to the enhanced program or to usual care with a brochure. The pilot's true endpoints are feasibility questions: can the practices recruit, will survivors accept the offer, and does the program run as designed? A full trial follows only if those answers are yes. The protocol matters because loneliness after cancer is common, harmful, and untouched by oncology's usual tools.
plos-pone-0351056:
Jeremy Gordon, John Chuang, and Giovanni Pezzulo asked how people plan a route before they start moving. Volunteers wore a virtual reality headset and could look around a map during a planning pause. Eye trackers recorded where each person looked, how far their gaze jumped, and how long it rested at each spot.

Early looking was wide and fast, then narrowed as a plan took shape. Fixations grew longer and jumps grew shorter near the end of planning. Spots that mattered most for joining parts of the map drew the most attention. People who planned in deeper steps did better only on the hardest maps. The pattern fits planning that breaks a big trip into smaller sub goals.
plos-pone-0351156:
Kethmany Ratsavong and colleagues studied why toddlers stay undernourished in city districts of Vientiane, Laos, where food is generally available. A survey of three hundred and thirty three mother and child pairs in two districts was followed by deep interviews with forty seven caregivers to explain the numbers.

About twenty seven percent of children under two were stunted, fourteen percent underweight, and four percent wasted, while five percent were overweight. Better nourished children had caregivers who drew advice from many sources and turned knowledge into daily practice. Caregivers of undernourished children leaned mainly on clinics. Practical demos and videos that build cooking and feeding skill may beat leaflets alone.
plos-pone-0351556:
Sex hormones shape joint health, and osteoarthritis may partly reflect their signals gone wrong. Yishu Wang and colleagues mined public gene datasets for hormone-linked genes that also change in osteoarthritic tissue, in this 2026 PLOS One bioinformatics study.

Genes altered in disease were crossed with hormone-associated candidates, then a network method picked the disease-relevant set. Three machine learning models voted for the hub genes at the center. Immune cell estimates showed how those hubs relate to the cells patrolling diseased joints. Checks against outside datasets and blood samples supported the picks. The authors offer the hubs as leads for hormone-aware arthritis research.
plos-pone-0351756:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask a surprising question about fat talk, the ritual of friends criticizing their own bodies to each other. Western research usually ties such talk to worse body image. Among about thirteen hundred female nursing students in Henan, China, the team measured fat talk, self-acceptance, and body image with standard scales.

All three moved together in the positive direction: more fat talk went with better body image, and with higher self-acceptance. A pathway analysis found that much of the link ran through self-acceptance, which accounted for over half of the effect, though its size was modest. The authors read the result culturally: in this setting, fat talk may work as bonding and mutual reassurance. They caution that context decides whether the same words harm or help, and that findings from one culture should not be exported carelessly.
plos-pone-0351856:
Moemen Khalifa and colleagues followed a hundred nine women through breast cancer radiotherapy that also treats nearby lymph nodes. They watched for a slow side effect: an underactive thyroid. Part of the gland sits close to the treatment field. Damage can surface months after treatment ends. Thyroid tests ran before treatment and six months after. Each woman's dose map across the gland was matched to her result.

About eight percent developed the thyroid problem in that window. Risk rose with the hottest dose to the gland. It rose most clearly with the share of the gland taking the highest dose band. Past a small share, the odds climbed steeply. A second cutoff marked the lobe nearest the treatment side. Planners now have concrete numbers for sparing the thyroid while they aim at the cancer.
plos-pone-0351956:
Mary Charlson, Martin Wells, and James Hollenberg present a population health tool in this 2026 study. The measure sums thirty-eight chronic conditions into one weighted score. It builds on the famous Charlson comorbidity tradition. Here the aim is prediction at population scale. The team calculated scores for over twenty-seven thousand Weill Cornell health plan members. Claims data covered six years, from 2016 to 2021, for employees and their families.

Scores from each year were tested against what happened next. The question was whether one number could flag future hospital admissions. Repeated admissions and the high costs that follow them counted too. A working score changes how health systems manage populations. Instead of reacting to crises, they can identify the highest-risk patients early. Interventions, from nurse check-ins to medication reviews, can then concentrate where preventable hospitalisations are likeliest. The study offers that score as a foundation for proactive, cheaper care.
plos-pone-0352156:
Manoj Kumar and Akshat Kumar Singh ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether India's soaring caesarean section rates are driven by medicine or by money. Using national family health surveys across two rounds and several states, they modeled which factors predict a surgical birth, from wealth and education to where the delivery took place.

The place of delivery towered over every other factor: giving birth in a private facility multiplied the odds of a caesarean several times over, and far more in some states than others. Wealth and education mattered mainly where public medical infrastructure was weak, largely by steering women into private care. The authors blame financial incentives in private practice and call for targeted policy to curb unnecessary surgery.
plos-pone-0352256:
Lixue Yang, Jiaxin Zhu, and Zengxin Zhang compare two ways of fine-tuning a large language model for specialist translation, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Their test bed was Chinese-to-English political text, an area where general models often stumble. One method retrained every parameter of the model; the other adjusted only a small part, using far less computing power.

On genuinely new political texts, neither method beat the untuned model in any consistent way. Only on test items drawn from the training material itself did both shine — a sign they had memorised overlap, not learned the domain. The sobering lesson: fine-tuning gains can be an illusion created by leaked test data.
plos-pone-0352356:
Larry Kessler and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether Americans answer national survey questions about cancer screening the same way twice. The National Health Interview Survey tracks screening for cervical, colorectal, breast, and lung cancers. Its results guide national health goals, so shaky answers would distort policy.

Nearly eighteen hundred adults from four health systems first answered the screening questions. Randomly chosen participants then repeated the survey one month or three months later. Agreement between the two rounds ranged from moderate to strong, depending on the question. Some people were set aside because they had new screening tests between rounds. Overall, the questions proved steady enough to trust for tracking national screening trends.
plos-pone-0352456:
Martina Pérez Serrano and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of how season changes the meat of wild male red deer in Spain. Thirty-two deer, taken by selective stalking with minimal stress, were harvested in September, January, April, and June. The team measured carcass traits and the chemistry of the loin muscle, expecting diet shifts and the effort of growing antlers to leave marks on the meat.

September deer carried the heaviest carcasses and the most fat within the muscle, while January and June animals were leanest. Tenderness, acidity after storage, and fatty acid makeup also shifted across the year. Mineral patterns pointed more to bone being drawn on during antler growth than to diet. The findings matter for hunters and game sellers judging meat quality by harvest date.
plos-pone-0352756:
Sora Kang and three colleagues ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether hospitals that patients rate highly are also the hospitals rated safest. The authors linked national patient experience survey results with independent safety grades for more than fourteen hundred American hospitals using 2023 data, then compared experience scores across the grade ladder.

Experience scores generally declined as safety grades worsened. Two measures stood out as independent predictors of a top safety grade: how well nurses communicated and whether patients would recommend the hospital. Scores for doctor communication oddly pointed the other way once other factors were included, which the authors treat cautiously. They conclude that patient experience and technical safety capture different but complementary sides of quality.
plos-pone-0352856:
Dominique Vincent-Genod and colleagues, including the MFM-Play Study Group, published this 2026 interview study of a therapy app for neuromuscular disease. The app turns a standard motor function test into a game, hoping children try harder and scores vary less between testers. Fourteen hospital therapists who had tried it discussed what helped and what blocked them.

Therapists liked the practical gains and the independence it gave patients, but training gaps, technical snags, and changed habits slowed adoption. Vincent-Genod concludes the app can work if hospitals support staff through a changed testing routine, not just hand over a tablet.
plos-pone-0353056:
Nishan Pokhrel and three colleagues watch four rescued tigers at Nepal's Central Zoo to see how captivity shapes their days, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Most of the zoo's tigers arrived after conflicts with people. Observers logged behaviour across summer and monsoon, during busy visiting hours and quiet ones, using scan sampling backed by camera footage.

The tigers spent most of their time asleep or resting. Visitor crowds stirred both sexes into more pacing and drinking, while quiet hours brought rest. Females explored and paced more than the largely sedentary males, and a recently rescued female played most of all. Long-term captives paced repetitively — a pattern keepers read as stress, and a prompt to enrich enclosures.
plos-pone-0353156:
Yichuang Luo, Fang Wang, and Xiaohu Liu present this 2026 PLOS One computer vision paper on following objects through video reliably, even when they are hidden briefly or move fast. Their method upgrades a leading segmentation model whose memory of earlier frames can accumulate errors. The upgrade estimates uncertainty about each object's appearance and motion and uses it to decide what the model should remember, with separate long-term and short-term memory handling.

Across five standard video benchmarks the method beat previous state-of-the-art systems, with the largest gains in scenes involving occlusion and objects reappearing after vanishing. The authors argue that tracking what a model is unsure about, not just what it sees, is the key to segmenting crowded, fast-changing video.
plos-pone-0353356:
Salem Mgammal Al-Ameri and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on transformer bushings. These fittings carry wires through a transformer's wall. They are a frequent source of breakdowns. The team modeled one bushing's electrical fingerprint in software. That fingerprint is its frequency response. They then varied the model's inner capacitance to mimic three faults. The faults were wear, surface dirt, and physical damage.

Each fault left a distinct pattern in the fingerprint. The authors mapped those patterns for future diagnosis. A second, physics-based model showed how electric fields shift under each fault. That explains why the patterns form. Together, the two approaches give utilities a way to spot bushing faults early. Early warning can keep a transformer in service.
plos-pone-0353456:
Nuha Al-Aghbari authored this 2026 PLOS One study asking whether two routine blood tests taken at hospital admission can predict which COVID-19 patients will die. Albumin, a protein tied to nutrition and organ reserve, and blood urea, a kidney-related waste measure, are cheap and widely available. The analysis covered more than a thousand adults treated at a single tertiary hospital.

About a quarter of the patients died in hospital. Those who died arrived with lower albumin and higher urea, and both measures still predicted death after accounting for age, other illnesses, and inflammation markers. Each step up in urea raised the odds of death, while higher albumin was protective. The author argues these simple tests add useful warning information beyond the usual inflammation measures.
plos-pone-0353556:
Tae Wan Kim and seven colleagues ask a stark question. Do patients who reach intensive care already in shock fare worse when their lungs fail? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It came from South Korea. They reviewed nearly three thousand five hundred adults. All had acute respiratory failure. All were treated at one major hospital between 2019 and 2023. Shock meant needing drugs to support blood pressure on arrival.

Nearly one in five patients arrived in shock. Their intensive care death rate was close to half. For the others it was under a fifth. The gap survived statistical adjustment for other risks. The pattern held across illness severity. It held across breathing-support types too. Shock on arrival, the authors argue, is a simple early warning sign.
plos-pone-0353756:
Limin Fang and four colleagues survey shoppers about what makes them buy plant-rich foods, in this 2026 PLOS ONE pilot study. Drawing on three theories of consumer behaviour, they modelled seven influences, from personal attitude and cultural setting to packaging design and the information on the label. Survey answers were fitted into a structural model linking each factor to buying intention and to healthy eating behaviour.

All seven factors pushed buying intention upward, but packaging's practical features pulled hardest, ahead of personal needs and food information. Product-side variables beat consumer-side ones overall. Intention then carried part of the effect into actual healthy eating. For food brands, the lesson is blunt: the packet may matter as much as the pitch.
plos-pone-0353856:
Mats Eriksson and four colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for watching the brains of newborns and their mothers at the same moment, during a routine painful procedure. Babies in intensive care endure repeated blood tests, and parents soothe them with skin contact, breastfeeding, and singing — but what that comfort does inside the brain is unknown. Twenty mother-baby pairs will be studied during a planned heel or vein blood draw.

Light-based scanners on both heads will record whether their brain activity synchronises, while heart rhythms, skin conductance, and the mother's gaze are tracked too. Pain will be scored from the baby's behaviour. The study aims to explain, in brain terms, why a parent's presence is medicine.
plos-pone-0353956:
Wen-Yu Jao and three colleagues compare two modern diabetes drug families for an unexpected side benefit, in this 2026 PLOS ONE database study. Both drug types control blood sugar and calm inflammation, which made researchers wonder whether they also protect joints. Using a huge multi-hospital record system, the team matched over four hundred and fifty thousand new users of one family against the same number starting the other.

Users of the first family, the SGLT2 blockers, developed osteoarthritis less often over five years than users of the GLP-1 medicines, especially in the knee. They also needed fewer major joint injections, though joint replacement rates matched. The authors call for trials to test whether the difference is real.
plos-pone-0354156:
Khadivi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, survey wild Persian irises growing in the mountains of Markazi Province, Iran. This ornamental flower is prized by gardeners, yet how much its wild plants vary from place to place was little known. Knowing that variation helps protect the species and pick the best plants for breeding.

The team measured dozens of traits, from flower size to color, in seventy-eight plants gathered from seven areas. Variation was wide: flower width, petal length, and other features differed a lot between plants. Statistical grouping sorted the plants into four clear families of form. Traits tied to flower size moved together closely, and a few traits best predicted overall flower width. Ten standout plants with fine flowers are named as breeding candidates. The survey gives growers and conservation workers a first map of what this wild iris has to offer.
plos-pone-0354256:
Marwa S Ibrahim and Ibrahim Naqid study wound infections in diabetic patients in Duhok Province, Iraq, in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Diabetes raises the risk of wound infection, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a frequent, drug-resistant cause. The team collected wound swabs from one hundred and forty-one adult patients over about a year.

The bacterium was found in close to forty-five percent of samples, making it a common cause here. Most patient traits showed no link, but leg wounds carried clearly higher risk, and body weight and job status also mattered. Isolates resisted many standard drugs, while colistin and carbapenem drugs kept the best activity. Early detection and careful drug choice are essential, they conclude.
plos-pone-0354356:
Klinga and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study in Sweden, follow health and social care leaders through a training program in person-centred leadership. Such leadership, which treats staff and patients as partners, is meant to spread person-centred care, but evaluations of the training are scarce. Thirteen leaders were asked what changed in how they lead.

Leaders described growth on three levels: leading themselves, leading their teams, and developing their workforce, all in a more person-centred direction. Three themes named the shift: enable co-creation, live as you learn, and strive for equal relations. None of it happened automatically. Leaders needed backing from their own bosses, time to coach, and work methods that share power, both during the course and after. The authors argue training budgets are wasted if organizations do not also build those surrounding conditions.
plos-pone-0354456:
Partho Bosu and co-authors run a computer-only search for drug leads against acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer where faulty cell growth crowds out healthy blood making. Starting from a public gene dataset, they found hundreds of genes behaving differently in the disease and mapped which ones sit at network hubs. Two hub proteins with known shapes became their docking targets.

Virtual screening built shape models for compounds that might block those targets, then filtered candidates for drug-like behavior and safety before detailed docking. A couple of compounds bound tightly in simulation and stayed stable in motion tests. Bosu and colleagues stress that these are candidates for lab testing, not proven drugs, and offer them as starting points for chemists.
plos-pone-0354756:
Caoyan Xu and seven co-authors published a pig genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They compared Chinese pig breeds with Western breeds, which differ in how much fat is marbled through the meat. Fat inside the muscle shapes taste, and breeders care about what controls it at the gene level.

Xu's team combined gene activity data with protein data to trace the control networks behind that marbling. The two breed groups turned out to use different sets of switches. Knowing which networks differ gives breeders clearer targets when they select animals, and it helps explain why the same feed can yield lean meat in one breed and rich meat in another.
plos-pone-0354856:
Alexa Pohl and co-authors scoped the research on how transportation shapes cancer screening and the stage at which cancer is found. Millions of Americans miss care each year for want of a ride. Their 2026 review searched five databases for quantitative patient-level studies across two decades and kept about one hundred after quality checks.

Screening studies slightly outnumbered stage studies in the final set. Measures of transport exposure fell into families: travel time and distance, help needed to make the trip, public transit, vehicle access, and patients' own sense of distance. Comparing those families exposed inconsistent measurement across the field. Pohl and colleagues recommend shared measures so future studies can actually be combined.
plos-pone-0355056:
Robert Ramirez-Garcia leads a 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper on reading short DNA pieces called oligonucleotides. These short strands, usually under three hundred letters, are vital for genome engineering and for storing digital data in DNA. Long DNA sequencing has advanced hugely, but accurate checks of short strands lagged behind.

The method, OligoSeq, pairs two tricks to make single strands readable on nanopore sequencers, which read DNA by electrical signals. One trick copies the strand; the other builds its mirror partner. Anchor matches then pin down the likely original sequence. The authors show nanopore reading with these steps is the most cost-effective route for checking strand quality, length, and variation.
plos-pone-0355156:
Agnieszka Drozdowska-Szymczak and co-authors outline in 2026 a study of whether a brain injury protein in cord blood can flag oxygen shortage in babies whose growth slowed late in pregnancy. The protein rises after injury to the central nervous system from low oxygen. Full term pregnancies with slowed growth will be compared with normally grown pregnancies after delivery.

Cord blood will be tested for the protein plus acidity and related measures, and blood flow scans just before birth will add context. The team will check whether protein levels track flow and blood gas results. As a protocol, it reports plans and approvals, not findings.
plos-pone-0355556:
Esther Ríos-Albert and co-authors analysed how key university figures across six European countries talk about sexual harassment. How leaders define the problem shapes whether victims report it and how institutions respond. Their 2026 study interviewed ninety informants, from student representatives to equality officers, and read the transcripts with critical discourse methods.

Informants described harassment as many-sided, spanning physical, verbal, non-verbal, and online acts. Accounts returned again and again to crossed boundaries, missing consent, and power gaps. The quoted title line calls it a hierarchical transgression. Definitions ranged from rule-based to experience-based to mixed, varying with gender and job role. The authors argue shared language is a first step toward shared response.
plos-pone-0355856:
Patrinee Traisathit and colleagues examined whether dirty air shortens survival for leukaemia patients in northern Thailand. They studied just over six hundred people with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia diagnosed across two decades. Their 2026 analysis split patients into children, adolescents and young adults, and older adults.

Survival fell steeply with age: about two-thirds of children lived five years, against very few older adults. Patients who died had breathed higher levels of fine particles and other pollutants, most clearly among children. High fine-particle levels were tied to greater death risk in the youngest group. Traisathit and colleagues argue air quality belongs in leukaemia care planning for the region.
plos-pone-0355956:
Joshua De Soyza leads a team of five checking whether a standard lung severity score works in a genetic lung disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency damages lungs and often brings bronchiectasis, chronically widened airways. A widely used severity index predicts death, hospitalization, and flare ups in ordinary bronchiectasis, but it had never been tested in this population. The team applied it to one hundred ninety-eight registry patients in Birmingham, nearly all with the severe genotype and most with COPD alongside.

The index sorted patients meaningfully. Survival differed significantly across its severity bands, exactly what a prognostic tool must do. The team also probed whether scores tracked lung function decline and quality of life measures. Validation in a rare disease subgroup matters because trials and clinics borrow tools from common diseases on faith. Here, at least for prognosis, the borrowed tool earned its place.
plos-pone-0356056:
Yaseen Al-Mulla mapped frankincense trees in Oman's Dhofar region using satellite images and the trees' light fingerprints. Frankincense resin is valuable, and the source tree matters ecologically and commercially, yet its spectral signature was barely studied. The 2026 study gathered field spectra across the visible and infrared range and matched them to high-resolution satellite bands.

A spectral matching method separated frankincense from surrounding vegetation far better than a simple greenness cutoff, which overstated cover. Overall mapping accuracy passed ninety percent. Three deep learning detectors were also tried on the imagery; the best found about seven hundred trees with strong precision and recall. Al-Mulla presents the workflow as a base for monitoring this prized species.
plos-pone-0356356:
Xinyuan Wang and Zhenyang Zhang examine what makes software developers in China actually follow data protection rules, in this 2026 survey study. Working from deterrence theory, they asked whether developers' awareness of data law shapes their compliance directly. They also asked whether it works indirectly, through how certain and how severe developers believe punishment to be. The analysis used structural models fitted to survey responses. Workplace compliance culture was tested as a further influence on those pathways.

Legal awareness promoted compliant behavior both directly and through perceived sanctions, with the certainty of being caught mattering more than the severity of the penalty. A strong compliance culture boosted awareness's effect on perceived certainty, though its boost to perceived severity was weakly supported. The authors advise regulators to invest in visible, consistent enforcement and companies to build cultures where rules feel real, rather than relying on harsh penalties.
plos-pone-0357156:
Chunmeng Wang and three colleagues fuse several photographs into one image that keeps both shadow and shine, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Scenes with bright skies and dark corners defeat a single exposure. Their system, MEF-TBN, splits the work among three cooperating branches. One reads fine local detail. One models the whole scene's structure with a transformer. The third restores natural color, which fusion methods often bleach or distort.

The branches produce weight maps that decide, pixel by pixel, which exposure should speak. A merging stage refines the local and global judgments together before the final blend. Against nine established fusion methods, the system topped most technical sharpness measures and swept the human perception oriented scores, while placing second on structural similarity. For phone cameras and medical imaging alike, the work shows that giving color its own dedicated branch pays off in pictures that look right, not just measure well.
plos-pone-0357756:
Emmanuel Daniel, Saada A. Seif, and Walter C. Millanzi published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on how new mothers in Tanzania's Kilimanjaro region keep their babies warm. Newborns lose heat fast in their first month, yet most research describes facility routines rather than what mothers do. The authors interviewed twelve post-natal mothers in depth at public facilities in 2024 and analyzed conversations for themes.

Four practice themes emerged. Mothers wrapped babies in multiple layers of cotton cloth and prepared clothing before delivery. They warmed rooms with heating or even lighting. They kept babies in constant skin-to-skin contact and breastfed promptly. And they massaged babies with oil and delayed bathing, both believed to protect warmth. These home-grown practices, the authors say, largely match clinical guidance, so health education should reinforce rather than replace them, and facilities should support skin-to-skin care and warm rooms.
plos-pone-0357956: Costa and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how the brain reacts to faces within fractions of a second. They recorded early electrical responses from the scalp. The title reports that these responses reflect prediction errors weighted by how precise the brain expects a face feature to be. Such work tests a leading theory of how the brain builds what we see.
plos-pone-0358056:
Chloe B Rodgers and three colleagues publish a recipe for growing pigment cells from sheep eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Uveal melanocytes, the dark cells lining the eye's middle coat, matter for eye biology and melanoma research. They are notoriously hard to isolate from human or primate tissue. Sheep eyes, plentiful from abattoirs, had never been developed as a source. The team set out to build the missing protocol.

They dissected donor eyes, lifted out the uveal tract, and freed the cells with successive enzyme treatments. The isolates proved to be genuine melanocytes, making pigment and switching on the expected genes. The cells froze, thawed, and regrew reliably. They also grew better in one commercial medium than in the recipe used for human cells. The group further worked out how to raise the cells as three dimensional spheres. A practical supply of these cells is now documented.
plos-pone-0358356:
Kantika Yadav leads a team of six setting out a study of healthy aging among tribal communities in Jharkhand, India, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Tribal elders age early: hard physical labor and undernutrition pull functional decline into the forties, and life expectancy lags the national picture. Mainstream elder care models rarely fit tribal culture, and research on this population is scarce. The protocol describes a two phase project across twenty-five villages, enrolling five hundred twenty adults aged forty-five and over.

First, a needs assessment will measure daily functioning, quality of life, and the burden of long term and infectious disease. Then the team will build, with the communities, a culturally grounded model of integrated local care, and test whether it is feasible and acceptable. The aim is care that starts before old age officially begins and speaks the language, literally and culturally, of the people it serves.
plos-pone-0358456:
Zafer Gayretli led a team of eight authors studying future sport managers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Sport management students need communication skills, but turning talk into ventures takes something more. The team tested whether career awareness sits in the middle, carrying the effect of communication skill into entrepreneurial tendency.

Gayretli's mediation model shows how self-knowledge can turn the ability to communicate into the drive to build enterprises. Universities training sport managers can act on that chain: teach students to read their own career options, not only to speak well. Entrepreneurship courses often treat skills as direct levers. A mediator like career awareness explains why the same skill course lifts some students and leaves others flat.
plos-pone-0358556:
Jakia Sultana Mim leads a team of six identifying what brings Bangladeshi mothers to skilled hands at delivery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A doctor, nurse, or midwife at the birth remains one of the strongest protections against maternal and newborn death. The team mined the 2022 national demographic and health survey with classical statistics and machine learning side by side, hunting the factors that separate attended from unattended births.

About sixty-eight percent of women delivered with a skilled attendant. Education towered over the other predictors: mothers with higher schooling had roughly four times the odds of skilled attendance of mothers with none. Household wealth, antenatal care visits, and urban residence each added their own lift. The machine learning models sharpened classification and confirmed the same leading variables. The policy reading is plain: schooling and antenatal contact are the roads by which skilled care reaches the delivery room.
plos-pone-0358656: Elmas and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how expectations shape body senses. People locate touch on their skin and sense where their limbs rest. The team found that prior expectations, shaped differently for each sense, steer both kinds of judgment. How the brain blends expectation with signal is a basic question with links to pain, prosthetics, and virtual touch.
plos-pone-0358756:
Zachary S Kelso, Madeleine C Snyder, and Samuel J Gershman report a failed attempt to teach flatworms a simple lesson, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Planarian worms are prized for regenerating body parts, and old experiments claimed they could learn to link light with shock, claims that later fed notorious memory transfer stories. The team tried to reproduce that basic conditioning in two species, using both the historical recipe and a modernized version.

Computer vision scored the worms' movements to keep judgment free of human bias. Across protocols they found no evidence of learning at all. The null result undercuts the classic procedures rather than the worms themselves. The authors urge future researchers to build tasks around what planarians naturally do. Only then, they argue, should anyone dig for the molecular basis of memory. Honest failures like this one clear ground that shaky classics left cluttered.
plos-pone-0359156:
Franziska Rees and Oliver Wilhelm wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about planetary health knowledge, what people know about the links between human health and the state of the planet. The authors develop a test for measuring that knowledge and evaluate its psychometric quality, whether it measures reliably and fairly.

The test is taxonomy-based, built from a structured map of the subject rather than random questions. Without a sound measuring tool, schools and campaigns cannot tell whether their teaching works. Educators and public health communicators working on climate and health literacy are the readers who need such an instrument.
plos-pone-0359656:
Nehal Ali published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It reappraises gene modules in peripheral blood that were linked to ADHD, sets of genes whose activity moves together in blood samples. The reappraisal puts the graph-based network analysis behind those modules through strict validation.

Blood-based gene modules raise hope for a simple ADHD test, but network methods can invent convincing-looking patterns from noise. Re-checking them rigorously, and asking whether they are biologically coherent, protects the field from chasing artifacts. Psychiatric genetics researchers are the readers for a validation that may either strengthen or shrink earlier claims.
plos-pone-0359856:
Yang-Tao Chen and co-authors measured in 2026 the burden of inflammatory bowel disease across Asia, and projected it to 2050. Inflammatory bowel disease, mainly Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, was once considered a Western condition, but cases have climbed across Asia with changing diets and cities. Their analysis draws on the 2023 Global Burden of Disease study and covers the years 1990 to 2023.

The authors chart how common the disease has become, country by country, and model where it is heading by mid century. Those projections tell Asian health systems to prepare clinics, specialists, and budgets for a patient group that barely existed a generation ago. The study marks a shift in the map of chronic digestive disease.
plos-pone-0360056:
Zacharie Tsala Dimbuene and Hugues Sampasa-Kanyinga wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on child nutrition. It studies malnutrition among children in the vast Democratic Republic of the Congo, where undernutrition remains widespread. Their data come from that country's demographic and health survey from 2023–24.

The method is a Bayesian Gaussian regression analysis, a statistical approach that estimates how factors relate to malnutrition while stating uncertainty openly. Survey-based national estimates help aid agencies and the Congolese health ministry see where need is greatest. Readers in global nutrition policy can compare these results with figures from neighboring countries facing similar pressures.
plos-pone-0360156:
Prakash Chellamuthu and co-authors investigated in 2026 how heat treatment settings affect the wear behavior of a hybrid aluminium composite. The material blends an LM26 aluminium alloy with graphite and fly ash, aiming for a light metal that resists friction better. How such a composite performs against rubbing and wear depends strongly on how it was heat treated.

The team used a Taguchi-TOPSIS approach, a structured optimization method that finds the best combination of settings from a limited set of experiments. Their subject, tribological performance, covers friction, wear, and lubrication where surfaces meet. Light, wear resistant aluminium parts serve engines and machinery, and using fly ash, an industrial byproduct, adds a recycling benefit if the recipe holds up.
pmc-1262556:
Auvert, Taljaard, Lagarde, and co-authors report a randomised trial testing whether male circumcision lowers HIV risk. Earlier observational work had hinted at protection, but only a controlled trial could test the claim fairly. The ANRS 1265 trial ran among the general population in South Africa.

More than three thousand uncircumcised young men, aged in their late teens to mid-twenties, took part and were assigned by chance to groups. Comparing infection rates between groups could show whether the procedure itself cut risk. The trial became a landmark input to later HIV prevention policy in high-burden regions.
pmc-13198056:
Viola Westfal and Maximilian von Heyden ran a 2026 online trial of brief prevention messages on child sexual abuse. Prevention needs public grasp and less stigma, yet the topic stirs strong feelings and false beliefs. The team tested whether a single short exposure could shift knowledge, attitudes, or intent to seek facts.

More than two thousand adults in Spain and Portugal were sorted into four groups. Three got short videos: teaching-based, humanizing with empathy focus, or humanizing with prevention focus. A fourth got neutral content. All message groups felt a short dip in positive mood and a slight rise in arousal. Stigma, knowledge, openness, and intent did not shift. No rebound harm appeared. Single exposures seem too weak alone.
pmc-13200056:
John I Ogbu and colleagues tested sesame seed extract on male fertility in rats in a 2026 study. Male factors drive about half of infertility cases. Natural food products draw interest as helpers, so the team gave rats water-based sesame extract for thirty days and added computer modeling of its compounds.

Two dose groups and recovery groups were compared with controls. Extract raised organ weights, sperm count and shape quality, and two key fertility hormones. Computer screening flagged four compounds, including two fatty acids, as likely actors. Their predicted targets cluster in pathways tied to cell survival and oxidative defense, with good binding fits. Short exposure and modeling limits temper the claims.
pmc-13203056:
Sterile lab mice may be missing the microbes that train human immunity, and a 2026 study headed by Edyta A Szurek gives them a dose of soil. The research article builds a model in which local soil-derived microbiota colonize lab mice, then checks immune and disease outcomes.

Lasting colonization by Gram-negative microbes, above all, shifted immune responses toward calmer patterns throughout the body. Regulatory T cells and IL-10 producing cell groups expanded in the colonized animals. Those changes protected the mice against colitis, obesity, diabetes, and sepsis in the noted experiments, and extended health span and lifespan, backing more nature-like models for immune research.
pmc-13236756:
Bugea and colleagues review ten years of cases where root canal work accidentally opened into the sinus. The roots of upper back teeth sit close to the maxillary sinus, so drilling or filling can sometimes break through into it. The team searched a decade of practice records from more than ten thousand treated upper premolars and molars.

They describe which teeth were involved, where the openings occurred, and how patients fared over the long term. Such openings are uncommon but can seed sinus trouble if missed. A ten-year map of real cases helps dentists judge how often this happens, which teeth carry the risk, and what follow-up keeps patients safe.
pmc-13237556:
Ferreira de Carvalho and colleagues describe a pituitary tumour that produced three hormones at once. The patient, a woman of forty-two, lost weight, felt her heart racing, stopped having periods, and slowly grew the enlarged features of acromegaly. Her tumour belonged to the PIT-1 family, which can make thyroid, growth, and milk hormones, though rarely all in active form together.

Together those secretions caused an overactive thyroid driven from the brain, excess growth, and raised prolactin at once. Untangling which hormone explains which symptom is the clinical puzzle. Cases like this teach hormone doctors to suspect a multi-hormone tumour when one label cannot cover the whole picture.
pmc-13242356:
Sharma's team at PGIMER Chandigarh plead the case of borderline intellectual functioning in India. The group, roughly IQ seventy to 85, comprises perhaps an eighth of the public. Neither ICD-11 nor DSM-5 lists it as a disorder. Planning, memory, and adaptive deficits are still steady.

Around forty percent also live with mental illness, often masked by their low scores. India's 2024 benefits gazette scores this band at 25 percent, below the forty percent benefit threshold. Aid, exam perks, and job quotas thus stay out of reach. The piece urges naming the group, training, and research funds.
pmc-13242456:
Fernanda de Paula Eduardo and colleagues documented mouth problems in patients receiving CAR-T cell therapy at a referral center. Their case series appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. CAR-T therapy works well against stubborn blood cancers but brings heavy immune side effects, and oral complications in these patients are rarely reported. The team reviewed medical and dental records for ten patients treated during 2024 and 2025.

Dry mouth, opportunistic infections, dental pain, and taste changes were the main findings, while the mouth sores many expected did not appear. Dental care centered on easing symptoms, preventing new infections, and watching for hidden dental trouble during the low-immunity period. The authors argue that a full dental check before treatment is essential, since quiet infections can flare when white cell counts crash. They also call for standard oral assessment routines in CAR-T programs.
pmc-13243756:
Liping Chen and colleagues characterized a troublesome outcome of childhood squint surgery: eyes that drift inward after being corrected for drifting outward. Their review of cases from 2016 to 2024 appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. Sixty patients developed this consecutive esotropia, and the team split them by their original operation: thirty-four had both outer eye muscles loosened, while twenty-six had a loosening-plus-tightening procedure.

The two-muscle loosening group more often showed a V-pattern, where the eyes' alignment changes between looking up and down. That group also carried a higher focusing-convergence ratio, meaning their eyes crossed more when focusing up close. pmc-13244956:

pmc-13245056:

pmc-13245756:

pmc-13247256:

pmc-13247656:

pmc-13249956:

pmc-13250756:

pmc-13253656:

pmc-13253756:
Masaru Uto and colleagues study a special itch in atopic dermatitis in a 2026 paper. Atopic dermatitis is a long-term skin disease with strong itching. pmc-13255456:

Rates were similar in women and men, and higher in patients over 45 than in younger ones. The authors urge regular uric acid checks for these patients.
pmc-13260656:

pmc-13263956:
Cristobal Castillo-Aliaga and colleagues published a 2026 study of feline leukemia virus in the guigna, a small wild cat of Chile and Argentina. The virus is common in pet cats and can spill into wild cats, with harsh effects. The team asked where guigna infections come from.

pmc-13266756:
Mario Shuchleib Cukiert and colleagues present a 2026 case report on rebuilding facial skin after cancer surgery. At one month the skin was healthy, the mouth closed well, and the look was judged good. The authors praise the method for matching skin color and texture.
pmc-13267556:
Yinping Han and Junlin Zhou present a 2026 case report and literature review on a rare cervical cancer that returned after ten years. Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the cervix is an uncommon, aggressive cancer. Their patient, a 60-year-old woman, had the cancer found after abnormal bleeding a decade earlier. She had surgery to remove the womb and ovaries but declined added drug or radiation treatment.

pmc-13269956:
Sindhuja Earagolla and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 67-year-old man treated at home with oral antibiotics for suspected pneumonia. Instead of improving, he developed fever, cough, weight loss, and worsening breathing. A repeat chest X-ray showed growing lung cloudiness.

pmc-13270256:

pmc-13271056:

Chance of response dominated, carrying 62 percent of the decision weight, followed by quality of life during response at 14 percent. pmc-13271356:

pmc-13272256: Myriam Lauren de Graaf is first named author on a 2026 correction notice for a 2025 article in Biological Cybernetics. That article covered how decreased spinal inhibition leads to plainer locomotor patterns, meaning less varied movement patterns. The correction concerns math notation in the original article. It notes a related sentence in the methods section. No results or conclusions are discussed in the notice.
pmc-13273156:

pmc-13273256:

pmc-13273856:

pmc-13274156:

pmc-13274256:

pmc-13274856:

pmc-13275156:

pmc-13275756:

pmc-13275956:

pmc-13276356:

pmc-13277156:

pmc-13277356:

pmc-13277756:

pmc-13278456:

pmc-13279656:

pmc-13279956:

pmc-13280456:

pmc-13280656:

pmc-13281156:

pmc-13281856:

pmc-13282056:

pmc-13282256:

pmc-13282356:

pmc-13282456:

pmc-13282856:

pmc-13282956:

pmc-13287156:

pmc-13288056:

pmc-13288356:

pmc-13289256:

pmc-13289356:

pmc-13289456:

pmc-13289656:

The authors stress these zones are exploratory, not firm cutoffs.
pmc-13290556:

pmc-13291356:

pmc-13291556:

pmc-13291656:

Gaps span gender, place, wealth, career stage, and language. Travel limits and thin funding deepen those gaps. The authors call the pattern a diplomatic monoculture. pmc-13291756:
Writing to the editor in 2026, Luo Ruiyu, Zhao Changjiang, and Li Yufei respond to a review by Zhong and colleagues on platelet-rich plasma for pattern hair loss. pmc-13292256:

pmc-13292356:

pmc-13292656:

pmc-13292756:

pmc-13292856:

Four compounds look most promising as starting points for new drugs, though body handling tests are still needed.
pmc-13293656:

pmc-13293756:

pmc-13294056:

pmc-13294156:

pmc-13294356:

pmc-13294856:

pmc-13295156:

pmc-13295656:

pmc-13296156:

pmc-13299256:

pmc-13301956:

pmc-13302756:

pmc-13303456:

pmc-13303556:

pmc-13304156:

pmc-13306356:

pmc-13306956:

pmc-13307156:

pmc-13307356:

pmc-13308656:

pmc-13309356:

pmc-13309456:

pmc-13309556:

pmc-13310056:

pmc-13310956:

pmc-13311056:

pmc-13311756:

pmc-13311956:

pmc-13312156:

pmc-13312456:

pmc-13314456:

pmc-13315856:

pmc-13316056:

pmc-13316156:

pmc-13318856:

pmc-13318956:

pmc-13319956:

pmc-13320356:

pmc-13320456:

pmc-13320556:
Bernhard Nagler and Thomas Staudinger reply in a 2026 letter to comments on their study of blood pressure drugs after lung support with a membrane oxygen machine. Their methods tried to allow for those effects within a backward looking design.
pmc-13323056:

pmc-13323556:
Zheqing Hu and co-authors explain stubborn mucus plugs in large airways, in a 2026 review covering cystic fibrosis, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Swollen submucosal glands hold a huge mucus reservoir, and their output can overwhelm the surface of big airways.

Their flush-load model blames imbalance: serous fluid from glands, the flush, falls short of hydrating heavy mucins, the load, so osmotic pressure collapses the cilia and seals the airway. Each disease tips the balance its own way, through faulty ion channels, type 2 inflammation or growth-factor driven remodelling. pmc-13325156:
Servet Askin, Nevin Çankaya, and Halim Yılmaz tune microwave digestion settings for measuring heavy metals in apricot in a 2026 study. Apricots are widely eaten, and toxic metals in them need exact measurement to judge risk.

pmc-13325256:
Zubaer Hossen and co-authors review how artificial intelligence is reshaping farm biotechnology in a 2026 article. Growing populations and climate stress squeeze yields, and AI tools promise faster, sharper decisions from messy farm data.

Applications span crop breeding and gene editing, genomic selection, pest and disease spotting, soil and nutrient care, and livestock work. The authors also chart fast growth in commercial patents beside academic output. Worries include who owns farm data and whether poor regions get left behind by the digital divide. Quantum computing is flagged as a coming frontier.
pmc-13327856:
Zebing Si and co-authors build an explainable fracture forecast for weak bones in a 2026 study from South China. They gathered 1,125 hospitalized patients with osteoporotic fractures who had bone density scans at one hospital between 2019 and 2025. From each record they drew 73 clinical, lab, and imaging features.

pmc-13328256:
Xin Wang and co-authors review diet, gut microbes, and the gut-brain axis in mental disorders in a 2026 article. Gut microbes shape immunity, metabolism, and hormone balance, and diet is a chief lever on that community. Imbalance has been tied to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, depression, autism, and ADHD.

Routes from gut to brain include immune signaling, the vagus nerve, microbe-made chemicals, and control of the blood-brain barrier. Human proof still lags animal work, tangled by genes, diet variety, medicines, and lifestyle. The authors weigh precision nutrition, probiotics, and stool transplants with care, urging mechanism-first, personal strategies rather than blanket claims for microbe therapies.
pmc-13331456:
Afnan Chaudhry and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a young man found unresponsive after taking at least 600 mg of propafenone along with other drugs. His heart tracing showed a sustained wide-complex fast rhythm, and his blood work showed severe acid build-up and kidney injury.

Propafenone blocks sodium channels, and the team treated that effect with an intravenous sodium bicarbonate drip aimed at mild alkalemia, plus close supportive care in intensive care. Within an hour the abnormal rhythm settled, the QRS complex narrowed, and sinus rhythm returned, with tracings still improving over the next day. The authors present QRS width as a live gauge of poisoning severity and argue for early bicarbonate treatment in this kind of overdose.
pmc-13332456:
Miguel Duran and co-authors map how the brain's central amygdala handles GLP-1 drugs in a 2026 mouse study. Medicines such as those used for diabetes and weight loss cut appetite through the brain, but which circuits they recruit directly has been unclear.

Using fiber photometry, the team watched the central amygdala light up quickly and durably after a dose of the GLP-1 agonist Exendin-4, an effect blocked by a GLP-1 blocker given beforehand. pmc-13334556:
Victor Udoewa wrote a 2026 essay on Black liberation futures and what he calls an ethics of hopelessness, the third part of a series on liberation system entanglements. Black liberation work spans community, health, education, work, food, and housing, all woven into wounded systems.

Reading futures work as spiritual practice through Black liberation theology, he describes Black Liberation Futures Design. There an impossible future means literally one that will never happen, and designing toward it anyway becomes the method. The essay challenges designers to drop hope as an entry requirement.
pmc-13335756:

pmc-13336356:

pmc-13336456:

Unifying recipe and route in one model points AI design at how metals are actually made.
pmc-13336856:

pmc-13339756:

pmc-13339856:

pmc-13341156:

pmc-13342956:

pmc-13343156:

pmc-13347656:

pmc-13348356:

pmc-13349956:

pmc-13350256:

pmc-13351556:

pmc-13352156:

pmc-13352256:

pmc-13352756:

pmc-13353056:

pmc-13354256:

pmc-13354956:

pmc-13355256:

pmc-13358756:

pmc-13359656:

pmc-13359756:

pmc-13361356:

pmc-13363356:

pmc-13363456:

pmc-13363656:

pmc-13363856:

pmc-13364656:

James Darmesteter, the great French orientalist, translated the Zend-Avesta, the scriptures of Zoroastrianism, into French. His Le Zend-Avesta presents the hymns, laws, and rituals of ancient Persia with a scholar's full notes. Zarathustra's religion reaches European readers here in one of its classic scholarly dressings.

Darmesteter treated the texts as a historian, dating layers and tracing ideas with care. French readers gained what Legge and Muller gave the English: a whole canon, weighed and explained. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, the work still serves students of Persian religion. It stands among the monuments of nineteenth-century Oriental scholarship.
tob-4056:
Volume three of the four-volume Secret Doctrine, edited after Blavatsky's death from her papers, continues her system into esoteric history and occult science. The same mixture of Eastern scripture, classical myth, and nineteenth-century research drives the argument. Initiates, secret doctrines, and hidden lineages of teachers stand closer to the surface here than in the cosmological first volume.

Fragmentary in places and formidable throughout, the volume reads partly as commentary and partly as workshop notes toward a system never finally settled. Readers working through the whole Secret Doctrine in order will find material here that later Theosophists treated as essential, and scholars treat as evidence of how the movement's teachings kept evolving.
tob-4156:
A. P. Sinnett's Esoteric Buddhism, first issued in 1883, carried Theosophy's teaching to thousands of ordinary readers. Sinnett, an Anglo-Indian editor, presented what he said the mahatmas taught: root races rising and falling, chains of worlds, and long cycles of rebirth for every soul.

The scheme claims to be Buddhism's inner meaning, hidden behind the outer doctrine. Scholars of Buddhism objected, then and since, yet the book's reach is beyond dispute. The New American Edition adds Sinnett's later introduction. More than any other single work, Esoteric Buddhism made Theosophy a household word in two hemispheres.
tocqueville-old-regime-bonner-1856:
Alexis de Tocqueville's The Old Regime and the Revolution appears in Henry Reeve's translation of 1856. Tocqueville, author of Democracy in America, turns to France's own revolution. His great claim is paradoxical: the Revolution completed the centralization it claimed to destroy. Kings had already leveled privilege and gathered power at Paris.

He shows how old taxes, intendants, and habits of tutelage survived 1789. The French, he argues, loved equality more than liberty. The book is his sequel and, some say, his masterpiece. It changed the study of the Revolution permanently. Reeve's version was the standard English text for years. Its insights still guide debate.
turgenev-rudin-1856:
Ivan Turgenev published Rudin in 1856, his first novel, the portrait of the superfluous man. The brilliant, ineffectual Rudin loves and loses in a tale of fine talk and failed action. Turgenev drew Rudin in part from Bakunin, the fiery exile he had known in Berlin.

Rudin descends on a provincial salon and dazzles it with talk of philosophy, progress, and the meaning of life. Natalya, the landowner's daughter, loves him and offers elopement, and at the pond he falters and bids her submit to fate. Lezhnev, the plain neighbor, states the verdict: Rudin's words are splendid and his will a hollow reed in the wind of life. Years later Rudin dies on a Paris barricade, brave at last in a cause not his own country's quarrel of 1848. The novel fixed the type of the talking hero for Russian fiction.
un-ga-res-a-69-56:
Money spent on arms is money not spent on schools, farms, and health. That trade-off drives Resolution A/69/56, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Charter itself dreams of peace kept with the least drain of human and trade wealth on arms. The text recalls the 1987 world meeting on the link between disarmament and growth, and a chain of votes since 1994.

Each cut in arms, the Assembly argues, frees real wealth for the work of growth. States are urged to weigh that gain when they set their arms plans. The vote keeps alive an old claim of the poor world: that disarmament is not just a safety aim, but a growth aim too.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/56 (2014) restates the link between disarmament and development. The Assembly recalls the Charter's aim of maintaining peace with the least diversion of human and economic resources to armaments. It voices concern at rising global military spending. That spending could otherwise meet development needs. It urges the international community to devote part of the savings from disarmament agreements to economic and social development. It asks the Secretary-General to keep implementing the 1987 action programme on the subject. It seeks member states' reports on their own transfers.
un-sc-res-1156:
On 16 March 1998, the Council adopted Resolution 1156 on Sierra Leone. The country's elected president had come home on 10 March 1998. His return followed months in exile after a military coup. Sanctions set in October 1997 had cut off oil and fuel supplies to pressure the junta.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ends the ban on selling petroleum and fuel products to Sierra Leone at once. The other bans from 1997 stay in place for now. They will be reviewed as events unfold and after talks with the restored government. The Council also welcomes plans by the Secretary-General to propose a future United Nations role in the country.
un-sc-res-1356:
Aid workers in Somalia, a country with no working state for a decade, needed protective gear that the arms embargo banned. The embargo had been imposed by Resolution 733 in 1992. The Council restated that all states had to obey it in full. Resolution 1356, adopted unanimously on 19 June 2001, cuts two narrow gaps in that ban.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the ban would not cover protective clothing. Flak jackets and military helmets were named in particular. United Nations staff, journalists, and aid workers could bring such gear in for their personal use, for a limited time. A second gap covered non-lethal military equipment meant only for humanitarian or protective use. That gear could go in only when the sanctions committee had approved it in advance. The rest of the embargo stood untouched.
un-sc-res-1456: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 1456, entered in this catalog under the year 2003. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1556:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 1556 on Darfur on 30 July 2004. Attacks on villages by Janjaweed militias had driven more than a million people from their homes. Some 200,000 refugees had fled into Chad. China and Pakistan abstained on the vote.

The text demands that Sudan's government disarm the Janjaweed and bring its leaders to justice. The Secretary-General must report on progress within thirty days and each month after. The Council bans the sale of arms to armed groups working in Darfur. It also backs African Union monitors and presses all sides to reach a political deal fast.
un-sc-res-156: Resolution 156 deals with a report from the Americas. The Council adopted it on 9 September 1960. The vote was nine to none. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained. The report came from the head of the Organization of American States. It passed on the Final Act of a meeting. Foreign ministers of the American republics had held that meeting. The Council takes note of the report. It notes one part in particular. The ministers had agreed on measures regarding the Dominican Republic.
un-sc-res-1656: Resolution 1656 dates to 2006 in the Council's output, preserved here from the official record via English Wikisource. Many of these texts are brief, built to answer one question at one meeting. The entry keeps the whole answer, preamble and decisions together, exactly as it entered the record of the world's security body.
un-sc-res-1756: Security Council Resolution 1756 is held in this collection as a Wikisource copy of the UN's official record. The act is one of hundreds in the Council's numbered series, each addressing the peace and security business of its moment. Its text follows the settled pattern, findings first and operative decisions after, and is preserved in full.
un-sc-res-1856:
Resolution 1856 gave the Council's ruling on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, adopted on 22 December 2008. Rebel attacks in North Kivu had driven huge crowds from their homes. The LRA struck in Orientale, and fighting flared again in Ituri. Regional summits in Nairobi had just named facilitators to help end the crisis.

The Council extends the mission, called MONUC, until 31 December 2009, with up to 19,815 troops. Its duties are ranked in strict order. Guarding civilians comes first, then disarming Congolese and foreign armed groups. The mission may inspect mines, trade routes, and markets to cut support drawn from stolen resources. Army training and border watching follow in the list.
un-sc-res-256:
Israeli air attacks on Jordan were condemned again by the Security Council on 16 August 1968. Two massive air attacks on Jordanian territory had been large in scale and planned with care. They broke resolution 248 (1968), which had condemned an earlier Israeli action and warned that grave breaches of the cease-fire could not be tolerated.

The Council reaffirmed resolution 248 (1968) and its warning of further, more effective steps. It deplored the loss of life and the heavy damage to property. It held that planned and repeated military attacks endanger the keeping of the peace. The new attacks were condemned as a flagrant breach of the United Nations Charter and of resolution 248. Israel was warned that any repeat would make the Council duly weigh its failure to comply. The text is one link in a chain of warnings over the Jordan front raids.
un-sc-res-456:
UNDOF's mandate on the Golan Heights ran to another renewal in late 1979. On 30 November 1979 the Security Council extended the force until 31 May 1980. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission. The decision keeps the standard three-part shape. The parties must apply resolution 338 without delay. A report on the term is due at its close.

China again took no part in the vote. The observers kept their posts in the separation zone. They had watched the line between Israel and Syria since 1974. The Council treated the renewal as steady maintenance of a working truce. Six months at a time, the mission rolled forward.
un-sc-res-56:
On 19 August 1948, the Council acted on Jerusalem by adopting Resolution 56. The city's truce kept breaking down. Reports from the UN mediator told of attacks by armed bands. The Council had set the truce terms a month earlier and now spelled out who bears blame.

The Council points both sides back to those terms. Each party answers for regular and irregular forces under its control. Each must use every means to stop truce breaches by people under its sway. Anyone who breaks the truce must face a speedy trial. Reprisal is no excuse for breaking the truce. No side may gain ground or favor by violating it.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1156, adopted by the Security Council on 16 March 1998, responds to the restoration of democracy in Sierra Leone. It welcomes the return of the country's democratically elected president on 10 March 1998, after the military junta was driven from power. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminates with immediate effect the ban on selling petroleum and petroleum products to Sierra Leone imposed by Resolution 1132 (1997). The other 1132 prohibitions, including the arms embargo, are to be reviewed in light of developments and talks with Sierra Leone's government.

Nine years into the Somalia arms ban, the Council carved out two narrow gaps. On 19 June 2001, it adopted Resolution 1356 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. The ban, set by Resolution 733 in 1992, blocked all arms shipments to Somalia. Aid work in the country still went on, though.

The text first restates every state's duty to enforce the ban. It then frees two kinds of goods from the ban. Safety gear for personal use is one kind. Flak jackets and helmets for UN staff, press, and aid workers count here. Non-lethal gear for aid or guard use is the second kind. A sanctions panel must clear such gear in advance.

Foreign ministers meeting on 20 January 2003 issue a declaration on fighting terrorism, and the short resolution simply adopts the statement attached to it. The statement reflects the Council's shared position sixteen months after the September 2001 attacks.

Terrorism is called one of the gravest threats to peace and security, and all such acts are condemned without exception. The declaration warns of the growing danger that terrorists could gain nuclear, chemical, or biological materials, and of their use of modern technology and global finance. It demands stronger action to cut terrorist funding and to block links with organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal arms sales.

Darfur's humanitarian catastrophe drives Resolution 1556, adopted on 30 July 2004. Janjaweed militia attacks, including rape and forced displacement, had put hundreds of thousands of lives at risk. Over a million people needed aid, and up to 200,000 refugees had fled into Chad. Sudan had promised to disarm the Janjaweed and open access to relief.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Sudan disarm the Janjaweed and bring their leaders to justice, with a progress report in 30 days and monthly after that. It warns of further measures if Sudan fails. It bans the sale or supply of arms and related gear to all non-governmental groups in North, South, and West Darfur. It backs the African Union's monitors and protection force and urges states to fund and equip them. It also extends the political mission for Sudan by 90 days, to 10 December 2004.

Regional action on the Dominican Republic is placed on the United Nations record on 9 September 1960. The Organization of American States had sent the Council the record of a meeting of American foreign ministers. At that meeting, the republics had agreed to apply measures against the Dominican Republic. The Council's short text simply takes note of that report and the agreement it described.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended until 31 March 2006 in this text of 31 January 2006. The two-month renewal came just before a scheduled meeting of the Group of Friends on Georgia in Geneva on 2 and 3 February 2006. It kept the mission watching the Abkhazia ceasefire lines in place while the next stage of the peace process was prepared.

Congo's mission, MONUC, is extended until 31 December 2007 on 15 May 2007, with a defined mandate. Elections had completed the transition, but violence in Bas-Congo and Kinshasa in early 2007 showed how fragile security remained. Congo's government, it is stressed, bears the main duty for safety in its territory.

The mission's tasks centre on protecting civilians, supporting the new institutions, and helping reform the army and police. MONUC may use all necessary means, within its capacity and deployment areas, to carry out its mandate. The government is urged to extend state authority, disarm militias, and uphold the rule of law and human rights, as the mission begins planning for an eventual drawdown.

MONUC is extended at surge strength with the Kivus as its overriding priority in Resolution 1856, adopted on 22 December 2008. CNDP offensives had displaced masses of people in North Kivu. The LRA was attacking in Orientale. The temporary reinforcement authorized by Resolution 1843 (2008) was meant to let the mission reconfigure for civilian protection.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 31 December 2009 with up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. Protection of civilians under imminent threat is its first mandate task, concentrated in the east. MONUC must deter attacks on the Goma and Nairobi processes and coordinate operations with Congolese brigades against local and foreign armed groups. It must cut their support from illicit resource trade and monitor the arms embargo with no-notice inspections, seizing violating weapons. Training the Congolese army and supporting democratic institutions complete the mandate.

Iraq's oil-revenue fund is given its final wind-down date in Resolution 1956, adopted on 15 December 2010. The Development Fund for Iraq and its monitoring board, created by Resolution 1483 (2003), had channelled Iraq's petroleum export proceeds under international oversight. Iraq's government said it would request no further extensions and had a transition plan; its prime minister's letter is annexed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminates the Development Fund arrangements on 30 June 2011 and declares this the final extension. After that date, oil and gas export proceeds no longer go into the Fund. The Fund's proceeds transfer to the government's successor accounts. The monitoring board ends. The requirement that 5 percent of petroleum export proceeds go to the United Nations Compensation Fund established under Resolution 687 (1991) continues unchanged. The Secretary-General is to report every six months on the fund from 1 January 2012.

Resolution 256, adopted unanimously on 16 August 1968, condemns a fresh round of Israeli air attacks on Jordan. Both governments had written and spoken to the Council. Two massive air strikes on Jordanian territory had followed an earlier attack the Council condemned that March in resolution 248.

The Council reaffirmed that earlier text, with its warning that grave ceasefire violations cannot be tolerated. It deplored the loss of life and heavy property damage. It judged that planned, repeated attacks put peace itself at risk. And it condemned the new attacks as flagrant violations of the Charter, warning that a repetition would make the Council take Israel's defiance into account in earnest.

Resolution 356, adopted unanimously on 12 August 1974, recommends the Republic of Guinea-Bissau for United Nations membership. Its application, document S/11393, had been examined by the Council. The West African country had declared independence from Portugal in 1973 after an armed liberation struggle, and many states already recognized it before Lisbon did.

Recommending admission, the Council set up the General Assembly's vote to seat Guinea-Bissau. The step carried symbolic force: a movement that had fought Portuguese colonialism now took a place among member states. Portugal itself accepted Guinea-Bissau's independence weeks later, closing a war that had helped bring down the government in Lisbon that spring.

Fourteen members backed the Golan renewal in Resolution 456. China took no part in the vote. The decision came on 30 November 1979. The Secretary-General's report on the observer force, document S/13637, lay before the members. UNDOF's mandate between Israel and Syria was running out again.

The force won six more months, until 31 May 1980. The Council paired renewal with its familiar demand. Both parties had to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The Secretary-General owed a closing report. It would cover events and steps toward that 1973 settlement. By 1979 these renewals were a settled rhythm. They kept a thin blue line in place while diplomacy stalled.

Jerusalem was a battlefield in August 1948, during the first Arab-Israeli war. A UN truce was in force on paper, but violations kept coming. The UN Mediator sent reports describing the disorder. Resolution 56, adopted on 19 August 1948, laid down strict rules for both sides.

Each party was made answerable for regular and irregular forces alike. Neither side could excuse a breach as payback. No one could use a truce violation to win military or political ground. Parties had to stop violations within their control. Offenders had to face speedy trials and punishment. The rules built on Resolution 54, the truce order passed that July.
